## [Garvey’s views on Obeah/Superstition](link_9)

Posted on [April 30, 2026](link_9) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 8](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/obeah.jpg?w=168)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/ [link_9])

While sorting through the Garvey Research/Reference Library’s collection recently, a research document was discovered that made reference to Garvey being suspected of practising Obeah. Olive Senior’s Encyclopedia of Jamaican Heritage defines obeah as being, “**_The word used in Jamaica to denote witchcraft, evil magic or sorcery by which supernatural power is invoked to achieve personal protection or the destruction of enemies_**”. The document identified stated that Garvey had erected a statue of an African Queen on the property of his Jamaican residence, Somali Court, which raised suspicion. In an apparent move to break Garvey’s occult practices, the statue was stolen and found destroyed days later.

Why the assumption that Garvey was delving into the supernatural, though? Could it be because of his mystique or his perceived omnipotence? In his presentation as guest speaker at the 2014 staging of the Annual Marcus Mosiah Garvey Lecture at Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey, Prof. Robert Hill, renowned Garvey scholar, hypothesized that Garvey was accompanied by a fallen angel which contributed to his supposed magical and mystical powers. The idea that Marcus Garvey was involved in witchcraft or the supernatural seems to have been a persistent rumour perpetuated by his critics. One can only imagine that this was done in order to undermine his credibility.

These claims of Garvey indulging in obeah/witchcraft are unfounded. Based on his speeches and writings, it is obvious that Garvey held obeah in low regard. He grouped obeah with superstition and viewed them as backward practices. For instance, in a speech Garvey delivered at Edelweiss Park on July 10, 1932, titled, “**The new Jamaica and how we can build it**”, he said “**_Stop making obeah to be our national contribution; because this does your country no good, and anything that does not benefit your country will not benefit you_**”. Prior to this statement, in the same speech, he had said, “**_Your only production is the bananas and cocoanuts and these are not man-made, they are the creation of God; but everything resulting from the genius of man that shows the character of man you are without; you have nothing typical to show except obeah (laughter) and that has no effect_**”. In a report on Garvey by Inspector W.A. Orrett of the Falmouth Constabulary Office, dated March 14, 1928, Garvey was quoted as saying, “**_Black man goes to the obeah man to keep down his fellowman. Set duppy to give him big foot_**”.

Marcus Garvey generally spoke about **obeah/superstition**in a way that was **critical, dismissive and sometimes humourous.**He essentially treated obeah as something that could undermine racial upliftment efforts and distract from economic and political growth. However, his criticism of obeah should not be seen as a rejection of African heritage as he strongly promoted African identity and Black pride.

# About

Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey honours the memory and work of Jamaica’s First National Hero. Located at 76 King Street, Kingston, it is a cultural educational institution that speaks first to the needs of the surrounding communities, then to the rest of the nation, then to Africans in Africa and the Diaspora, and then to the rest of the world.

The primary mission of Liberty Hall is “To inform the public about the work of Jamaica’s First National Hero and to use his philosophy and opinions to inspire. excite and positively affect the self-identity of Jamaican people, while creating social and economic wealth.” This mission is supported through the activities of the various units within the organization, those being, the Marcus Mosiah Garvey Multimedia Museum, the Garvey Multimedia Centre, The Garvey Research/Reference Library and the Gift Shop.

Liberty Hall is a special project of the African Caribbean Institute of Jamaica/Jamaica Memory Bank which is a Division of the Institute of Jamaica, an Agency of the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport.

## [Garvey’s views on Obeah/Superstition](link_2)

Posted on [April 30, 2026](link_2) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/obeah.jpg?w=168)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/ [link_2])

While sorting through the Garvey Research/Reference Library’s collection recently, a research document was discovered that made reference to Garvey being suspected of practising Obeah. Olive Senior’s Encyclopedia of Jamaican Heritage defines obeah as being, “**_The word used in Jamaica to denote witchcraft, evil magic or sorcery by which supernatural power is invoked to achieve personal protection or the destruction of enemies_**”. The document identified stated that Garvey had erected a statue of an African Queen on the property of his Jamaican residence, Somali Court, which raised suspicion. In an apparent move to break Garvey’s occult practices, the statue was stolen and found destroyed days later.

Why the assumption that Garvey was delving into the supernatural, though? Could it be because of his mystique or his perceived omnipotence? In his presentation as guest speaker at the 2014 staging of the Annual Marcus Mosiah Garvey Lecture at Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey, Prof. Robert Hill, renowned Garvey scholar, hypothesized that Garvey was accompanied by a fallen angel which contributed to his supposed magical and mystical powers. The idea that Marcus Garvey was involved in witchcraft or the supernatural seems to have been a persistent rumour perpetuated by his critics. One can only imagine that this was done in order to undermine his credibility.

These claims of Garvey indulging in obeah/witchcraft are unfounded. Based on his speeches and writings, it is obvious that Garvey held obeah in low regard. He grouped obeah with superstition and viewed them as backward practices. For instance, in a speech Garvey delivered at Edelweiss Park on July 10, 1932, titled, “**The new Jamaica and how we can build it**”, he said “**_Stop making obeah to be our national contribution; because this does your country no good, and anything that does not benefit your country will not benefit you_**”. Prior to this statement, in the same speech, he had said, “**_Your only production is the bananas and cocoanuts and these are not man-made, they are the creation of God; but everything resulting from the genius of man that shows the character of man you are without; you have nothing typical to show except obeah (laughter) and that has no effect_**”. In a report on Garvey by Inspector W.A. Orrett of the Falmouth Constabulary Office, dated March 14, 1928, Garvey was quoted as saying, “**_Black man goes to the obeah man to keep down his fellowman. Set duppy to give him big foot_**”.

Marcus Garvey generally spoke about **obeah/superstition**in a way that was **critical, dismissive and sometimes humourous.**He essentially treated obeah as something that could undermine racial upliftment efforts and distract from economic and political growth. However, his criticism of obeah should not be seen as a rejection of African heritage as he strongly promoted African identity and Black pride.

## [JAMAICAN-BASED DANCERS IN THE UNIA](link_4)

Posted on [November 3, 2025](link_4) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 3](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/sagwa-bennett.jpg?w=444)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/ [link_4])

Marcus Garvey was a cultured man who used the Arts to empower Black people and build their character. He achieved this through the activities of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Cultural units were established in the performing arts and members of these units were given a salary.

Dance was one aspect of the Arts that the UNIA paid particular attention to. It played a significant role in the UNIA. It served not only as a means of entertainment, but also as a tool for cultural pride, unity and resistance. Dances and dance competitions were often held at Edelweiss Park and the Kingston Liberty Hall and they were used to liberate black people.

Garvey launched and/or supported the careers of several Jamaican-based dancers. Many of Jamaica’s top show dancers came out of the UNIA’s cultural units. These included Harold ‘**_Kid Harold_**’ Smith, Randolph ‘**_Ranny_**’ Williams and Arthur ‘**_Sagwa_**’ Bennett. The dance group, **_The Follies_**, was also a popular unit out of the UNIA.

**Harold ‘_Kid Harold’_ Smith**

Kid Harold was a prominent Jamaican tap dancer who was also a part of the comedy duo ‘**Harold and Trim’**. He was affiliated with the UNIA’s cultural programme at Edelweiss Park and he led a dance group called Butterfly Troupe. At Edelweiss Park he also trained aspiring dancers and sometimes served as a judge for the dancing contests hosted by the UNIA. Kid Harold had said that Garvey’s legacy in the field of dance was to provide some of the best professional dancers on the entertainment circuit.

**Randolph ‘_Ranny_’ Williams**

Ranny Williams is popularly known as an actor and comedian. However, he began his career as a dancer in the UNIA. He was first a backline dancer, then a frontline dancer and eventually a feature dancer with partners. Ranny was described as a good dancer and became a popular feature of the UNIA’s entertainment programmes.

**Arthur ‘_Sagwa_’ Bennett**

Sagwa Bennett was a dancer/performer with the UNIA who also worked as a dance trainer for a dance troupe. He appeared in many of the musical comedies produced by Ranny Williams.

**The Follies**

The most popular cultural unit of the UNIA was a dance group named the Follies. This was a group of dancers who performed choreographed Broadway-style pieces that incorporated mento-style movements. The Follies often performed in cabaret shows, musical revues and concerts. They also usually performed every Monday night at Edelweiss Park and at the monthly concerts there

## [Garvey supports reparations](link_7)

Posted on [August 29, 2025](link_7) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 4](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/reparations.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/08/29/garvey-supports-reparations/ [link_7])

The International Center for Transitional Justice (ICTJ) defines reparations as “… **_to acknowledge and repair the causes and consequences of human rights violations and nequality in countries emerging from dictatorship, armed conflict and political violence, as well as in societies dealing with racial injustice and legacies of colonization._**” Though Marcus Garvey did not use the actual term “**_reparations_**”, he was a strong advocate for restitution to people of African descent. He believed that this could be achieved through African redemption, racial solidarity and racial self reliance. Consequently, some of his tenets align with some of the principles of reparations.

**_Anti-Colonialism:_**

Garvey spoke and wrote extensively on the exploitative and undemocratic nature of colonialism, which included among other things, the political subjugation of the masses, economic exploitation, and racial segregation. He not only opposed colonialism in Africa and the Caribbean, but also its existence everywhere. He supported the nationalist movements in China, India, and the Eastern European states. Garvey said, **_“The British, the French, the Dutch, and others have raped Africa of her manhood and are now doing the same thing in India and the Far East… The Black man must awaken and claim his own.”_**

**_Restitution:_**

This refers to the restoration of something to its rightful owner. This includes freedom and rights, as well as property. Garvey believed that colonial authorities owed people of African descent a moral and historical debt. He said, **“_The white man has sinned against the black man for over four hundred years. He has deprived him of a knowledge of himself, he has robbed him of a country and has made him a slave, and then he has branded him as an inferior being. If the white man is honest, he will make the restitution that he can. If he is dishonest, then he must pay for it through the penalty of the Almighty God_.”**He asked for the return of what was robbed and exploited, including “our own civilization”.

**_Repatriation:_**

Thisgenerally refers to the return of something (or someone) to their country of origin. Garvey’s “Back to Africa” movement advocated for Black people in the diaspora to return to Africa and build an independent, powerful Black nation. Garvey said, **_“Our program is for the redemption of Africa. We are going to carry our people back home. We do not want to live among white men. We do not want to be subject to them. We want to build for ourselves. This is our chance to get a government, an empire of our own, and it is up to us to fight for that which is ours. We have given civilization to the world, and now they owe us a debt, and that debt will be collected.”_**

**_Economic self-sufficiency:_**

Garvey believed in **self-reliant****reparations****:** economic and institutional power through enterprises built by people of African descent. Garvey thus had economic empowerment as one of his aims towards the redemption of the Black race. Owning the means of production, and not just simply providing labour, was critical to black empowerment. At the heart of this economic scheme was also the formation of transnational economic linkages and of resource sharing within the race. Hence, there was the formation of a number of economic projects such as the Black Star Line, the Negro Factories Incorporated, the Negro World, The Black Man, and New Jamaican newspaper companies, the Edelweiss Amusement Company and other ventures.

However, Garvey still acknowledged that the colonial powers still **owed Black people access to capital and opportunity** after centuries of exploitation. Garvey said, **_“We are going to have our own businesses, our own ships, our own industries. That is what will repair the damage of slavery and injustice—not a gift from our oppressors, but power that we build ourselves. But the world owes us the chance and the capital to do it.”_**

Marcus Garvey was a strong advocate for racial justice and Black empowerment and made it clear that restitution must include land, freedom and control over one’s future. His philosophy and opinions not only support the reparations movement but formed the foundation of the cause.

## [One “Black” Church?](link_8)

Posted on [January 31, 2025](link_8) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 5](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/black-church-feature.jpg?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/01/31/one-black-church/ [link_8])

The Right Excellent Marcus Garvey was a spiritual man; in fact, he was Christian. He recognized that there is a God and that we should believe in Him. Despite his changing denominations throughout his lifetime, (from Methodist to Catholic) God remained a central, influential figure in Garvey’s life. In his poem, “**_The Everlasting Life_**”, the third verse says:

“**_It’s safer then to have one God_**

**_Whose life is first and ever so_**

**_And all the rest to live in Him_**

**_With all the good they ever had_** …”

Though religion played an important part of the work of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (U.N.I.A), it is important to note that Garvey never intended for the U.N.I.A to be a church nor did he intend for the U.N.I.A to adopt a church. In the editorial of the July 17, 1921 issue of the Negro World with headline, “**_U.N.I.A Favors All Churches, But Adopts None as U.N.I.A Church_**” it stated, “**_the U.N.I.A is not a church, and does not intend to be one. So far as the present signs are, there will be no church connected with the U.N.I.A.”_**However, this view did not negate Garvey’s belief that, “**_The Church is the most beneficent institution, the greatest civilizing agency;_**”

Garvey encouraged an African interpretation of Christianity, which dispelled the white/European interpretation of God being white. He saw the need to make religion relevant to the Black experience. Circa 1919, he met an aspiring priest named George Alexander McGuire who shared his views on black theology. Consequently, he appointed him as Chaplain-General for the U.N.I.A. However, whilst it seemed as if McGuire wanted the U.N.I.A to adopt the African Orthodox Church (AOC) as the official church of the U.N.I.A, Garvey, on the other hand, though he endorsed the idea of a “Black Church”, did not want to alienate anyone because of their religious belief. So, the AOC was never adopted by the U.N.I.A. though it was formed by clergy in the movement. Eventually, McGuire broke away from the U.N.I.A to focus on the development of the AOC that he founded in 1921.

Garvey’s resistance to having the U.N.I.A devoted to one Church was that it would cause division among the members. With practitioners of the many different denominations and faiths existing in the U.N.I.A, Garvey thought that forcing all the members to follow one religious doctrine would be disruptive to the movement. He recognized that religion could be a divisive force and as such, he tried to promote unity and support all faiths that promoted “Black” theology.

## [MARCUS GARVEY AND AMY ASHWOOD: A UNION OF LOVE AND ACTIVISM](link_11)

Posted on [December 23, 2024 February 12, 2025](link_11) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 6](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/12/23/marcus-garvey-and-amy-ashwood-a-union-of-love-and-activism/ [link_11])

On December 25, 1919, Marcus Mosiah Garvey, the charismatic leader of the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League (UNIA/ACL), married Amy Ashwood, a fellow activist and trailblazer in the early Pan-African movement. Their wedding, held at Liberty Hall in Harlem, New York, symbolized more than a personal commitment—it marked a powerful partnership in the shared struggle for African empowerment.

The ceremony, attended by allies and members of the UNIA, was a celebration of African heritage and the Pan-African ideals that both Garvey and Ashwood championed. Liberty Hall, a significant site for Garveyism and Black empowerment, was a fitting venue for this historic event. Their union reflected the merging of two passionate advocates dedicated to the liberation and upliftment of people of African descent.

**Visionaries in the fight for freedom**

Marcus Garvey, renowned for his pioneering work in Black Nationalism, envisioned a global movement where people of African descent could unite, reclaim their dignity, and achieve economic independence. Through initiatives like the Black Star Line and his iconic slogan, _“Africa for the Africans,”_ he inspired millions across the diaspora. His tireless efforts were fueled by a belief in self-reliance and the reclamation of cultural pride.

Amy Ashwood, equally formidable, was a staunch advocate for women’s rights and social justice. Born into a prominent Afro-Jamaican family, she was a founding member of the UNIA and a vocal supporter of Pan-Africanism. Ashwood’s advocacy extended beyond the political sphere to embrace education and cultural enrichment. Reflecting on her role, she once said, _“Women must be the guardians of our future, nurturing the seeds of knowledge and unity for generations to come.”_

**Challenges in Revolutionary Relationships**

Despite the promise of their union, the marriage faced significant personal and political challenges. Garvey’s unrelenting dedication to his work often kept him away, causing tensions between the couple. By 1922 their marriage had ended, but their shared mission endured. Garvey later married Amy Jacques, another influential UNIA figure, while Ashwood continued her activism independently.

Ashwood’s subsequent work, including the establishment of the International African Friends of Ethiopia, exemplified her unwavering commitment to African independence and unity. This period underscores how personal sacrifices often intertwine with the demands of revolutionary movements.

**A Legacy that endures**

Marcus Garvey and Amy Ashwood remain icons of the Black liberation struggle. Their wedding, held on Christmas Day at Liberty Hall, stands as a significant moment in the history of the Pan-African movement. It symbolizes the intersection of love, activism, and a vision for a better world.

Their work laid the foundation for much of the Pan-Africanist movement that continues to inspire generations. As Garvey famously said, _“A people without the knowledge of their past history, origin, and culture is like a tree without roots.”_ Their shared efforts ensured that future generations would remain deeply rooted in their heritage.

**Reflection and call to action**

The story of Marcus Garvey and Amy Ashwood invites us to reflect on the power of unity, resilience, and shared purpose in the face of adversity. How can we draw inspiration from their legacy to address today’s struggles for justice, equality, and empowerment? Let us honor their contributions by continuing to uplift and unite our communities.

Édouard Lock received international acclaim for his risky, virtuosic movement vocabulary. He began his choreographic career at the age of 20 and founded La La La Human Steps in 1980. He has created works for some of the world’s leading dance companies, including the Paris Opera Ballet, the Het Nationale Ballet of Holland, The Nederlands Dans Theater, the Cullberg Ballet, and the Royal Ballet of Flanders. He co-conceived and was artistic director for David Bowie’s world tour, Sound and Vision. He also collaborated with Frank Zappa on the Yellow Shark concerts. Various films have been made on Lock’s work including Le Petit Musée de Vélasquez directed by Bernar Hébert, and the documentary Inspirations by British director Michael Apted. The film adaptation of Amelia, directed by Édouard Lock, had its American premiere at the 2004 Tribeca Film Festival and its European premiere at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival. The film won its category at the Chicago International Film Festival, the Prague International Film Festival, and the Rose d’Or Festival in Switzerland, as well as winning two I.C.E. and two Gemini Awards for best direction and best editing. Édouard was named a Chevalier de l’Ordre National du Québec, is an Officer of the Order of Canada, and received a Governor General’s Award. ## [Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey: Celebrating 23 Years of Heritage, Service and Vision](link_2)

Posted on [September 29, 2026](link_2) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/liberty-hall.jpg?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/09/29/liberty-hall-the-legacy-of-marcus-garvey-celebrating-23-years-of-heritage-service-and-vision/ [link_2])

Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey (LH) celebrates its 23 rd anniversary on October 20, 2026. For 23 years, LH has stood as more than a historic building. It has been a living space of memory, education, culture, creativity and community: a place where the ideas and ideals of one of Jamaica’s most influential national figures continue to inspire new generations.

As Liberty Hall celebrates its 23rd anniversary, it is an opportunity not only to commemorate the journey so far, but also to reflect on the institution’s accomplishments and look ahead to the possibilities that the future holds.

**In the beginning …**

In 2002, through the collaborative efforts of a group of committed and influential individuals who formed the Friends of Liberty Hall, funds were raised locally and internationally to begin the restoration of LH. The actualization of the restoration was as a result of the efforts of the Friends of Liberty Hall as well as the then Ministry of Entertainment, Youth and Culture, the Jamaica National Heritage Trust and the Government of Jamaica. After an extensive refurbishing project, Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey opened on October 20, 2003.

**Honouring a legacy …**

At the heart of LH is the enduring legacy of Marcus Garvey, Pan-Africanist and Jamaica’s first National Hero, whose message of Black pride, self-determination, education, enterprise and collective advancement continues to resonate across Jamaica and the wider world.

Garvey understood the importance of creating spaces where people could gather, learn, organize and imagine a better future. Eventually, he established several spaces, worldwide, for the development and processing of ideas for intellectual and spiritual upliftment, and as shrines of ‘**_Negro inspiration and the cradle of Negro Liberation_**’. These places were called Liberty Halls.

Today, LH embodies that spirit and carries that heritage forward by preserving and interpreting Garvey’s contributions while connecting his ideas to contemporary Jamaican life.

**23 Years of Accomplishment …**

Over the past 23 years, LH has developed into an important cultural and educational institution. Its work has extended beyond preserving historical artifacts and telling the story of Marcus Garvey. It has created opportunities for people, especially young people, to engage with history, culture and creativity.

Through exhibitions, educational outreach programmes, public lectures, and community activities, LH has helped make Garvey’s ideas accessible and relevant. This is one of LH’s greatest accomplishments.

LH’s contribution extends into Jamaica’s cultural landscape. It has provided a platform for artists, educators, historians, researchers, students, community members and cultural practitioners. It has also created a bridge between past and present, reminding us that understanding where we come from can help us make more meaningful choices about where we are going.

Perhaps one of Liberty Hall’s most important responsibilities and accomplishments is its work with young people. The future of any cultural institution depends on its ability to inspire the next generation. By introducing young people to Marcus Garvey’s life, ideas and accomplishments, LH encourages them to think critically about identity, leadership, community and possibilities.

In a world filled with rapid technological change, social pressures and uncertainty, young people need spaces that encourage them to learn, create, question and dream. LH continues to be one of those spaces.

**Looking Toward the Future …**

As LH enters its next chapter, its 23rd anniversary is not simply a celebration of what has been achieved. It is also an invitation to imagine what comes next.

The future presents exciting opportunities for LH to deepen its role as a centre for heritage, education and innovation. Digital technology can make its collections, exhibitions and educational resources accessible to audiences far beyond its physical location. Partnerships with schools, universities, cultural organizations, artists and community groups can expand its reach and strengthen its impact. There is also an opportunity to connect Garvey’s principles with contemporary issues facing Jamaica, Africa and its diaspora, including entrepreneurship, education, cultural preservation, community development, technology and youth empowerment.

The challenge is not simply to preserve Garvey’s legacy, but to ensure that the legacy remains useful.

**23 Years and Still Moving Forward …**

Marcus Garvey’s vision was rooted in the belief that people and communities possess the power to shape their own destiny. LH carries that message into the 21st century by providing a place where history can inspire action, culture can encourage creativity, and education can open doors.

Its next chapter can build upon the foundation established over the past 23 years while embracing new audiences, new technologies and new ideas.

Twenty-three years is a milestone worth celebrating. It represents years of preserving history, sharing knowledge, supporting culture, engaging communities and keeping the story of Marcus Garvey alive for generations who did not have the opportunity to know him personally. However, perhaps the greatest measure of LH’s success is not simply how much it has preserved, but how much it continues to inspire.

As we celebrate 23 years of Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey, we celebrate a past that must be remembered, a present that must be engaged and a future that must be imagined. Just as Marcus Garvey challenged his generation to believe in the possibilities of a better tomorrow, LH will continue to challenge each new generation to learn from the past, believe in itself and help build the future.

LH is a project of the African Caribbean Institute of Jamaica/Jamaica Memory Bank, a division of Institute of Jamaica, an agency of the Ministry of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport.

**_Happy 23rd Anniversary, Liberty Hall._**

**_Twenty-three years of legacy. Twenty-three years of learning. Twenty-three years of culture, community and inspiration, and a future filled with even greater possibilities._**

## [People of African descent: recognition, justice and development](link_4)

Posted on [August 31, 2026 August 31, 2026](link_4) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 3](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/international-day-for-people-of-african-descent.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/08/31/people-of-african-descent-recognition-justice-and-development/ [link_4])

Monday, August 31, 2026 is the fifth commemoration of the International Day for People of African Descent (IDPAD) after its designation by the UN General Assembly on December 16, 2020. The observance is aimed at promoting “**_greater recognition and respect for the diverse heritage, culture and contribution of people of African descent to the development of societies, and to promote respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms of people of African descent._**” It also serves to highlight the persistent issues of discrimination encountered by these communities.

This commemoration is another manifestation of Marcus Garvey’s work as it intentionally resonates with the first official proclamation of Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World at Marcus Garvey’s First International Convention of Negro Peoples of the World in New York on August 31, 1920. This Declaration of Rights included twelve (12) points of grievance and fifty-four (54) demands. The demands called for social and political independence as well as focused on civil rights and equal opportunity in business, etc. They also sought the recognition of the UNIA as sovereign representative of the Black race. The Declaration served as a powerful assertion of rights, dignity, and equality at a time when colonialism, segregation, and racial bias were prevalent. It tackled important topics like fair treatment, access to education, political engagement, economic chances, and the ability of Black individuals to shape their own destiny.

IDPAD formed part of the declaration of the **_International Decade for People of African Descent_**, from 2015 to 2024, under the theme“**_People of African descent: recognition, justice and development_**”. The goal was to advance human rights, fight against racism and intolerance, and recognize the contributions of individuals of African descent globally, during this decade. However, despite the efforts to eradicate racism, much more work is left to be done as racism persists and evolves. In recognition of this the UN has declared a Second **_International Decade_****_for People of African Descent,_** established by General Assembly Resolution 79/193 in December 2024. This decade, under the same theme as the first, spans January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2034. This new decade aims to build on the previous one by addressing systemic racism and improving the rights and inclusion of people of African descent.

In her article, **Black Communities Celebrate International Day for People of African Descent,** Gift Ikeke sums up the significance of the theme, **_People of African descent: recognition, justice and development_**as follows:

“**_Recognition_** means acknowledging the immense contributions people of African descent have made across science, art, politics, literature, and every other field of human achievement, contributions that have too often gone uncredited. **_Justice_** means confronting the ongoing legacies of slavery, colonialism, and systemic racism that still shape outcomes in health, policing, education, and economic opportunity today. **_Development_** means pushing for real investment and inclusion, not just symbolic recognition, in the communities the day is meant to hono[u]r.”

With the challenges that still exist globally with respect to racism and equality, IDPAD should not only serve as a remembrance but also as an opportunity to contemplate the disparity that may arise between global human rights pledges and their true application in policies, institutions, and daily experiences.

## [Copyright and Liberty Hall: Balancing access and responsibility](link_5)

Posted on [May 20, 2026](link_5) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 4](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/picture1.png?w=399)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/05/20/copyright-and-liberty-hall-balancing-access-and-responsibility/ [link_5])

Copyright is a cornerstone of the creative and intellectual world.It refers to the exclusive legal rights granted by the government to creators, such as authors,editors,composers,playwrights, and publishers, to publish,produce, sell, or distribute their work. These works may be literary,musical, dramatic, artistic, or otherwise. At the same time,institutions like libraries and museums exist to provide public access to knowledge and culture,much of which is protected by copyright. This creates an important balance between access and protection, one that institutions must navigate carefully every day.

The Garvey Research/Reference Library (GRRL) and the Marcus Mosiah Garvey Multimedia Museum (MMGMM) at Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey are no exception.Both house a wide range of materials. The Library collection includes books, journals,photographs, and audiovisual media, while the Museum incorporates photographs,audio recordings and videos into its multimedia exhibits. Given the nature of these collections, copyright plays a signiﬁcant role in shaping their operations.

**How Copyright Shapes Ope****rations**

Copyright directly inﬂuences how both the GRRL and MMGMM collect, display,and share materials.

**Collection:**

Both units must ensure that all acquisitions comply with copyright law. This means that materials added to both collections must be legal copies. As a result,Liberty Hall’s Donation Policy requires that all donated works meet these standards.

**Display:**

The way items are displayed often depends on the terms under which they were acquired.For instance,rare books or manuscripts may come with restrictions that limit how and where they can be viewed, sometimes requiring special conditions for access.

**Sharing:**

Copyright also governs how materials can be shared with the public.In the Museum, certain works cannot be photographed due to copyright restrictions. Similarly,in the Library, some materials, such as manuscripts and unpublished works, cannot be copied.However, the Library operates within legal frameworks,like Fair Dealing, which allow limited use of copyrighted materials for education,research, and criticism.

**Risk****of****Copyright Infringement**

Like all cultural institutions, the GRRL and MMGMM are susceptible to copyright infringement.Infringement occurs when the exclusive rights of a copyright holder are violated without permission. In Jamaica, the Copyright Act of 1993 outlines these protections and deﬁnes infringement.Within the context of the Library and Museum,infringement can occur in several ways:

**In the Library:**

**Photocopying**: Allowing users to copy substantial portions of copyrighted works beyond legal limits can result in infringement.

**Exhibitions and Publications:** The Library regularly mounts exhibitions, creates digital displays for social media, and produces newsletters and promotional materials.Using copyrighted images, text, or music without permission in these formats would constitute infringement.

**In the Museum:**

**Exhibitions:** Similar to the Library, the Museum uses images, text, and sound recordings.Unauthorized use of copyrighted material in exhibits is a risk.

**Digitization:** Converting materials into digital formats can introduce copyright concerns. Sharing digitized content publicly without verifying copyright status or obtaining permission may infringe on the rights of creators.

**Staying****Within the Law**

To fulﬁll their mission while respecting copyright laws,the GRRL and MMGMM follow clear guidelines, such as:

![Image 5](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/blog/)– Allowing limited photocopying strictly for private study and research.

![Image 6](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/blog/)– Seeking permission before using copyrighted material in exhibitions,publications, or on social media.

![Image 7](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/blog/)– Educating patrons on the proper and lawful use of copyrighted works.

The GRRL and MMGMM remain committed to providing access to knowledge and cultural heritage while upholding the legal and ethical responsibilities that protect creators. By carefully navigating copyright laws, they ensure that they honour both the public’s right to access information and the creators’right to control and beneﬁt from their work.

## [Garvey’s views on Obeah/Superstition](link_7)

Posted on [April 30, 2026](link_7) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 8](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/obeah.jpg?w=168)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/ [link_7])

While sorting through the Garvey Research/Reference Library’s collection recently, a research document was discovered that made reference to Garvey being suspected of practising Obeah. Olive Senior’s Encyclopedia of Jamaican Heritage defines obeah as being, “**_The word used in Jamaica to denote witchcraft, evil magic or sorcery by which supernatural power is invoked to achieve personal protection or the destruction of enemies_**”. The document identified stated that Garvey had erected a statue of an African Queen on the property of his Jamaican residence, Somali Court, which raised suspicion. In an apparent move to break Garvey’s occult practices, the statue was stolen and found destroyed days later.

Why the assumption that Garvey was delving into the supernatural, though? Could it be because of his mystique or his perceived omnipotence? In his presentation as guest speaker at the 2014 staging of the Annual Marcus Mosiah Garvey Lecture at Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey, Prof. Robert Hill, renowned Garvey scholar, hypothesized that Garvey was accompanied by a fallen angel which contributed to his supposed magical and mystical powers. The idea that Marcus Garvey was involved in witchcraft or the supernatural seems to have been a persistent rumour perpetuated by his critics. One can only imagine that this was done in order to undermine his credibility.

These claims of Garvey indulging in obeah/witchcraft are unfounded. Based on his speeches and writings, it is obvious that Garvey held obeah in low regard. He grouped obeah with superstition and viewed them as backward practices. For instance, in a speech Garvey delivered at Edelweiss Park on July 10, 1932, titled, “**The new Jamaica and how we can build it**”, he said “**_Stop making obeah to be our national contribution; because this does your country no good, and anything that does not benefit your country will not benefit you_**”. Prior to this statement, in the same speech, he had said, “**_Your only production is the bananas and cocoanuts and these are not man-made, they are the creation of God; but everything resulting from the genius of man that shows the character of man you are without; you have nothing typical to show except obeah (laughter) and that has no effect_**”. In a report on Garvey by Inspector W.A. Orrett of the Falmouth Constabulary Office, dated March 14, 1928, Garvey was quoted as saying, “**_Black man goes to the obeah man to keep down his fellowman. Set duppy to give him big foot_**”.

Marcus Garvey generally spoke about **obeah/superstition**in a way that was **critical, dismissive and sometimes humourous.**He essentially treated obeah as something that could undermine racial upliftment efforts and distract from economic and political growth. However, his criticism of obeah should not be seen as a rejection of African heritage as he strongly promoted African identity and Black pride.

# People of African descent: recognition, justice and development

Posted on [August 31, 2026 August 31, 2026](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/08/31/people-of-african-descent-recognition-justice-and-development/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/international-day-for-people-of-african-descent.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/08/31/people-of-african-descent-recognition-justice-and-development/)

Monday, August 31, 2026 is the fifth commemoration of the International Day for People of African Descent (IDPAD) after its designation by the UN General Assembly on December 16, 2020. The observance is aimed at promoting “**_greater recognition and respect for the diverse heritage, culture and contribution of people of African descent to the development of societies, and to promote respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms of people of African descent._**” It also serves to highlight the persistent issues of discrimination encountered by these communities.

This commemoration is another manifestation of Marcus Garvey’s work as it intentionally resonates with the first official proclamation of Declaration of Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World at Marcus Garvey’s First International Convention of Negro Peoples of the World in New York on August 31, 1920. This Declaration of Rights included twelve (12) points of grievance and fifty-four (54) demands. The demands called for social and political independence as well as focused on civil rights and equal opportunity in business, etc. They also sought the recognition of the UNIA as sovereign representative of the Black race. The Declaration served as a powerful assertion of rights, dignity, and equality at a time when colonialism, segregation, and racial bias were prevalent. It tackled important topics like fair treatment, access to education, political engagement, economic chances, and the ability of Black individuals to shape their own destiny.

IDPAD formed part of the declaration of the **_International Decade for People of African Descent_**, from 2015 to 2024, under the theme“**_People of African descent: recognition, justice and development_**”. The goal was to advance human rights, fight against racism and intolerance, and recognize the contributions of individuals of African descent globally, during this decade. However, despite the efforts to eradicate racism, much more work is left to be done as racism persists and evolves. In recognition of this the UN has declared a Second **_International Decade_****_for People of African Descent,_** established by General Assembly Resolution 79/193 in December 2024. This decade, under the same theme as the first, spans January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2034. This new decade aims to build on the previous one by addressing systemic racism and improving the rights and inclusion of people of African descent.

In her article, **Black Communities Celebrate International Day for People of African Descent,** Gift Ikeke sums up the significance of the theme, **_People of African descent: recognition, justice and development_**as follows:

“**_Recognition_** means acknowledging the immense contributions people of African descent have made across science, art, politics, literature, and every other field of human achievement, contributions that have too often gone uncredited. **_Justice_** means confronting the ongoing legacies of slavery, colonialism, and systemic racism that still shape outcomes in health, policing, education, and economic opportunity today. **_Development_** means pushing for real investment and inclusion, not just symbolic recognition, in the communities the day is meant to hono[u]r.”

With the challenges that still exist globally with respect to racism and equality, IDPAD should not only serve as a remembrance but also as an opportunity to contemplate the disparity that may arise between global human rights pledges and their true application in policies, institutions, and daily experiences.

# JAMAICAN-BASED DANCERS IN THE UNIA

Posted on [November 3, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/sagwa-bennett.jpg?w=444)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/)

Marcus Garvey was a cultured man who used the Arts to empower Black people and build their character. He achieved this through the activities of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Cultural units were established in the performing arts and members of these units were given a salary.

Dance was one aspect of the Arts that the UNIA paid particular attention to. It played a significant role in the UNIA. It served not only as a means of entertainment, but also as a tool for cultural pride, unity and resistance. Dances and dance competitions were often held at Edelweiss Park and the Kingston Liberty Hall and they were used to liberate black people.

Garvey launched and/or supported the careers of several Jamaican-based dancers. Many of Jamaica’s top show dancers came out of the UNIA’s cultural units. These included Harold ‘**_Kid Harold_**’ Smith, Randolph ‘**_Ranny_**’ Williams and Arthur ‘**_Sagwa_**’ Bennett. The dance group, **_The Follies_**, was also a popular unit out of the UNIA.

**Harold ‘_Kid Harold’_ Smith**

Kid Harold was a prominent Jamaican tap dancer who was also a part of the comedy duo ‘**Harold and Trim’**. He was affiliated with the UNIA’s cultural programme at Edelweiss Park and he led a dance group called Butterfly Troupe. At Edelweiss Park he also trained aspiring dancers and sometimes served as a judge for the dancing contests hosted by the UNIA. Kid Harold had said that Garvey’s legacy in the field of dance was to provide some of the best professional dancers on the entertainment circuit.

**Randolph ‘_Ranny_’ Williams**

Ranny Williams is popularly known as an actor and comedian. However, he began his career as a dancer in the UNIA. He was first a backline dancer, then a frontline dancer and eventually a feature dancer with partners. Ranny was described as a good dancer and became a popular feature of the UNIA’s entertainment programmes.

**Arthur ‘_Sagwa_’ Bennett**

Sagwa Bennett was a dancer/performer with the UNIA who also worked as a dance trainer for a dance troupe. He appeared in many of the musical comedies produced by Ranny Williams.

**The Follies**

The most popular cultural unit of the UNIA was a dance group named the Follies. This was a group of dancers who performed choreographed Broadway-style pieces that incorporated mento-style movements. The Follies often performed in cabaret shows, musical revues and concerts. They also usually performed every Monday night at Edelweiss Park and at the monthly concerts there

# MARCUS GARVEY AND AMY ASHWOOD: A UNION OF LOVE AND ACTIVISM

Posted on [December 23, 2024 February 12, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/12/23/marcus-garvey-and-amy-ashwood-a-union-of-love-and-activism/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/12/23/marcus-garvey-and-amy-ashwood-a-union-of-love-and-activism/)

On December 25, 1919, Marcus Mosiah Garvey, the charismatic leader of the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League (UNIA/ACL), married Amy Ashwood, a fellow activist and trailblazer in the early Pan-African movement. Their wedding, held at Liberty Hall in Harlem, New York, symbolized more than a personal commitment—it marked a powerful partnership in the shared struggle for African empowerment.

The ceremony, attended by allies and members of the UNIA, was a celebration of African heritage and the Pan-African ideals that both Garvey and Ashwood championed. Liberty Hall, a significant site for Garveyism and Black empowerment, was a fitting venue for this historic event. Their union reflected the merging of two passionate advocates dedicated to the liberation and upliftment of people of African descent.

**Visionaries in the fight for freedom**

Marcus Garvey, renowned for his pioneering work in Black Nationalism, envisioned a global movement where people of African descent could unite, reclaim their dignity, and achieve economic independence. Through initiatives like the Black Star Line and his iconic slogan, _“Africa for the Africans,”_ he inspired millions across the diaspora. His tireless efforts were fueled by a belief in self-reliance and the reclamation of cultural pride.

Amy Ashwood, equally formidable, was a staunch advocate for women’s rights and social justice. Born into a prominent Afro-Jamaican family, she was a founding member of the UNIA and a vocal supporter of Pan-Africanism. Ashwood’s advocacy extended beyond the political sphere to embrace education and cultural enrichment. Reflecting on her role, she once said, _“Women must be the guardians of our future, nurturing the seeds of knowledge and unity for generations to come.”_

**Challenges in Revolutionary Relationships**

Despite the promise of their union, the marriage faced significant personal and political challenges. Garvey’s unrelenting dedication to his work often kept him away, causing tensions between the couple. By 1922 their marriage had ended, but their shared mission endured. Garvey later married Amy Jacques, another influential UNIA figure, while Ashwood continued her activism independently.

Ashwood’s subsequent work, including the establishment of the International African Friends of Ethiopia, exemplified her unwavering commitment to African independence and unity. This period underscores how personal sacrifices often intertwine with the demands of revolutionary movements.

**A Legacy that endures**

Marcus Garvey and Amy Ashwood remain icons of the Black liberation struggle. Their wedding, held on Christmas Day at Liberty Hall, stands as a significant moment in the history of the Pan-African movement. It symbolizes the intersection of love, activism, and a vision for a better world.

Their work laid the foundation for much of the Pan-Africanist movement that continues to inspire generations. As Garvey famously said, _“A people without the knowledge of their past history, origin, and culture is like a tree without roots.”_ Their shared efforts ensured that future generations would remain deeply rooted in their heritage.

**Reflection and call to action**

The story of Marcus Garvey and Amy Ashwood invites us to reflect on the power of unity, resilience, and shared purpose in the face of adversity. How can we draw inspiration from their legacy to address today’s struggles for justice, equality, and empowerment? Let us honor their contributions by continuing to uplift and unite our communities.

## [JAMAICAN-BASED DANCERS IN THE UNIA](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/)

Posted on [November 3, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/sagwa-bennett.jpg?w=444)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/)

Marcus Garvey was a cultured man who used the Arts to empower Black people and build their character. He achieved this through the activities of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Cultural units were established in the performing arts and members of these units were given a salary.

Dance was one aspect of the Arts that the UNIA paid particular attention to. It played a significant role in the UNIA. It served not only as a means of entertainment, but also as a tool for cultural pride, unity and resistance. Dances and dance competitions were often held at Edelweiss Park and the Kingston Liberty Hall and they were used to liberate black people.

Garvey launched and/or supported the careers of several Jamaican-based dancers. Many of Jamaica’s top show dancers came out of the UNIA’s cultural units. These included Harold ‘**_Kid Harold_**’ Smith, Randolph ‘**_Ranny_**’ Williams and Arthur ‘**_Sagwa_**’ Bennett. The dance group, **_The Follies_**, was also a popular unit out of the UNIA.

**Harold ‘_Kid Harold’_ Smith**

Kid Harold was a prominent Jamaican tap dancer who was also a part of the comedy duo ‘**Harold and Trim’**. He was affiliated with the UNIA’s cultural programme at Edelweiss Park and he led a dance group called Butterfly Troupe. At Edelweiss Park he also trained aspiring dancers and sometimes served as a judge for the dancing contests hosted by the UNIA. Kid Harold had said that Garvey’s legacy in the field of dance was to provide some of the best professional dancers on the entertainment circuit.

**Randolph ‘_Ranny_’ Williams**

Ranny Williams is popularly known as an actor and comedian. However, he began his career as a dancer in the UNIA. He was first a backline dancer, then a frontline dancer and eventually a feature dancer with partners. Ranny was described as a good dancer and became a popular feature of the UNIA’s entertainment programmes.

**Arthur ‘_Sagwa_’ Bennett**

Sagwa Bennett was a dancer/performer with the UNIA who also worked as a dance trainer for a dance troupe. He appeared in many of the musical comedies produced by Ranny Williams.

**The Follies**

The most popular cultural unit of the UNIA was a dance group named the Follies. This was a group of dancers who performed choreographed Broadway-style pieces that incorporated mento-style movements. The Follies often performed in cabaret shows, musical revues and concerts. They also usually performed every Monday night at Edelweiss Park and at the monthly concerts there

## [Garvey’s views on Obeah/Superstition](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/)

Posted on [April 30, 2026](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/obeah.jpg?w=168)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/)

While sorting through the Garvey Research/Reference Library’s collection recently, a research document was discovered that made reference to Garvey being suspected of practising Obeah. Olive Senior’s Encyclopedia of Jamaican Heritage defines obeah as being, “**_The word used in Jamaica to denote witchcraft, evil magic or sorcery by which supernatural power is invoked to achieve personal protection or the destruction of enemies_**”. The document identified stated that Garvey had erected a statue of an African Queen on the property of his Jamaican residence, Somali Court, which raised suspicion. In an apparent move to break Garvey’s occult practices, the statue was stolen and found destroyed days later.

Why the assumption that Garvey was delving into the supernatural, though? Could it be because of his mystique or his perceived omnipotence? In his presentation as guest speaker at the 2014 staging of the Annual Marcus Mosiah Garvey Lecture at Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey, Prof. Robert Hill, renowned Garvey scholar, hypothesized that Garvey was accompanied by a fallen angel which contributed to his supposed magical and mystical powers. The idea that Marcus Garvey was involved in witchcraft or the supernatural seems to have been a persistent rumour perpetuated by his critics. One can only imagine that this was done in order to undermine his credibility.

These claims of Garvey indulging in obeah/witchcraft are unfounded. Based on his speeches and writings, it is obvious that Garvey held obeah in low regard. He grouped obeah with superstition and viewed them as backward practices. For instance, in a speech Garvey delivered at Edelweiss Park on July 10, 1932, titled, “**The new Jamaica and how we can build it**”, he said “**_Stop making obeah to be our national contribution; because this does your country no good, and anything that does not benefit your country will not benefit you_**”. Prior to this statement, in the same speech, he had said, “**_Your only production is the bananas and cocoanuts and these are not man-made, they are the creation of God; but everything resulting from the genius of man that shows the character of man you are without; you have nothing typical to show except obeah (laughter) and that has no effect_**”. In a report on Garvey by Inspector W.A. Orrett of the Falmouth Constabulary Office, dated March 14, 1928, Garvey was quoted as saying, “**_Black man goes to the obeah man to keep down his fellowman. Set duppy to give him big foot_**”.

Marcus Garvey generally spoke about **obeah/superstition**in a way that was **critical, dismissive and sometimes humourous.**He essentially treated obeah as something that could undermine racial upliftment efforts and distract from economic and political growth. However, his criticism of obeah should not be seen as a rejection of African heritage as he strongly promoted African identity and Black pride.

## [BLACK WOMEN OF VALOUR: Amy Ashwood Garvey](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/12/31/black-women-of-valour-amy-ashwood-garvey/)

Posted on [December 31, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/12/31/black-women-of-valour-amy-ashwood-garvey/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 3](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/amy-ashwood.jpg?w=350)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/12/31/black-women-of-valour-amy-ashwood-garvey/)

**_**\_“Women must be the guardians of our future, nurturing the seeds of knowledge and unity for generations to come.” – Amy Ashwood Garvey\_**_**

January 10, 2026 will mark the 129 th anniversary of the birth of Amy Ashwood, pan-Africanist, feminist, founding member of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) and first wife of Marcus Garvey.In a previous post here, the significance of her union with Marcus Garvey was discussed. However, too often is she remembered only in relation to him.Amy Ashwood Garvey deserves recognition in her own right as a radical thinker and international activist.

Ashwood was part of a family that was well-off resulting from her father owning bakeries in Port Antonio, Jamaica and Colon, Panama. This may have made her experience as a young, black girl in Jamaica, a little less intimidating. It was not until she attended Westwood High School in Trelawny, Jamaica, that her black consciousness was awakened. There she was exposed to history lessons about Africa, slavery and her African heritage. She also joined the Debating Club which honed her debating and oratorical skills. After leaving school, Ashwood engaged in several activities including organizing and participating debates at the East Queen Street Baptist Church. It was there that she met Garvey after defeating him in a debate. Their shared vision of a united and redeemed Africa brought them together and ended in them getting married on Christmas Day 1919 in New York. Unfortunately, their vision outlasted the marriage and they divorced a few years later in 1922.

Ashwood’s contribution to the UNIA and to Pan-Africanism is immeasurable. As a founding member of the UNIA, she played a crucial role in developing its initial principles and organizational framework, while also championing the concept of a unified Africa well before this notion became popular.Her involvement in such activities, at that time, was pioneering, particularly on the international scene, as women were not allowed to voice their opinions. She denounced gender marginalization and oppression within Black movements and insisted that women were central to liberation struggles.

Ashwood also gave lectures all over the Caribbean and West Africa, and was crucial in bringing Guyana’s Black and Indian communities together. She also played an instrumental role in unifying Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana’s first Black President, and his opponent, J. B. Danquah.

Amy Ashwood Garvey died in 1969, leaving behind a legacy of activism, resilience and empowerment for women. It is therefore, quite unfortunate, that despite all her significant contributions, the exact location of her grave in the Calvary Cemetery in Kingston, Jamaica is uncertain. More earnest efforts should be made to identify her grave and make it a monument; a physical reminder of her legacy.

## [GARVEY’S UTOPIA NOT REALIZED](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/09/29/garveys-utopia-not-realized/)

Posted on [September 29, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/09/29/garveys-utopia-not-realized/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 4](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/liberia.gif?w=300)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/09/29/garveys-utopia-not-realized/)

October 2025 marks 105 years since Marcus Garvey, through the UNIA, launched a $2 million Liberian Construction Loan with plans to repatriate Blacks to Liberia. It was Garvey’s vision to have persons of African descent return to Africa and work towards the liberation and development of Africa. Popularly known as the **_“Back-to-Africa”_** Movement, the aim was to have Blacks reclaim their heritage and form their own government, free of colonial influence.

When the search for a geographical base of the UNIA’s African colonization mission began, the options considered were Tanganyika, Ethiopia and Liberia. Liberia eventually proved to be the best option, possibly for the fact that it was already an independent African nation governed by Blacks. It could also have been because of the connection African-Americans had to Liberia, having been founded by freed African-Americans in 1822 through the American Colonization Society.

After deciding on Liberia as the country to settle and lay the foundations for the greater plan to liberate Africa, the UNIA sent its Auditor General, Elie Garcia, to Liberia to do a site visit and evaluate the situation there. The intent of the UNIA was conveyed by Mr. Garcia in his letter to the President of Liberia, dated June 8, 1920, where he stated that the UNIA’s intent was to:

*   Establish trade routes through a line of steamships, etc
*   Encourage emigration to build up the country
*   Transfer the UNIA’s headquarters to Liberia
*   Bring medical and scientific units to Liberia

By June 14 th, the President gave approval for the UNIA to settle in and assist in developing Liberia. However, Garcia had also sent a confidential report to Garvey about the unbecoming conditions in Liberia. Nevertheless, the plan to develop Liberia continued. By October 1920, the Liberian Construction Loan, which replaced the previous Liberian Liberty bonds promotion, was launched. The money was intended to be given to the Liberian government as a loan for the resettlement project. It was to finance construction and development in Liberia as well as to ship workers and materials there. When a UNIA delegation of six, including a technical team, went to Liberia in 1921, five hundred square miles of land was designated to the UNIA, by the Liberian government, for the establishment of UNIA colonies. Despite this, the government encouraged the delegation to keep the project and subsequent negotiations a secret due to pressure from American, British and French authorities.

In December 1923, a smaller UNIA delegation of three went to Liberia to iron out the details of the arrangement for the plan to immigrate to Liberia. Both parties came to an agreement after certain commitments were made and all that was left to do when the delegation left was the official signing of the agreement. Later, the plan was not realized owing to a series of unfortunate events. The most damaging of these was the Liberian government reneging on their verbal agreement with the UNIA.

At the same time the Liberian government was making arrangements with the UNIA, it was being courted by the U.S.-owned Firestone Rubber Company. Eventually, they entered into a contract with the company, unbeknownst to the UNIA. Consequently, the June 1924 delegation from the UNIA was denied entry to Liberia and the equipment that they brought with them, valued at approximately US $50,000, was confiscated. Additionally, the five hundred square miles of land that was promised to the UNIA was leased to Firestone for 99 years.

The actions of the Liberian government were very damaging. They derailed the plan to establish a base for the strategies to liberate the African continent, tarnished the reputation of the UNIA, deflated the morale of the members and most importantly, crushed Garvey’s dream of establishing his utopian colony in Africa.

## [Garvey supports reparations](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/08/29/garvey-supports-reparations/)

Posted on [August 29, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/08/29/garvey-supports-reparations/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 5](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/reparations.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/08/29/garvey-supports-reparations/)

The International Center for Transitional Justice (ICTJ) defines reparations as “… **_to acknowledge and repair the causes and consequences of human rights violations and nequality in countries emerging from dictatorship, armed conflict and political violence, as well as in societies dealing with racial injustice and legacies of colonization._**” Though Marcus Garvey did not use the actual term “**_reparations_**”, he was a strong advocate for restitution to people of African descent. He believed that this could be achieved through African redemption, racial solidarity and racial self reliance. Consequently, some of his tenets align with some of the principles of reparations.

**_Anti-Colonialism:_**

Garvey spoke and wrote extensively on the exploitative and undemocratic nature of colonialism, which included among other things, the political subjugation of the masses, economic exploitation, and racial segregation. He not only opposed colonialism in Africa and the Caribbean, but also its existence everywhere. He supported the nationalist movements in China, India, and the Eastern European states. Garvey said, **_“The British, the French, the Dutch, and others have raped Africa of her manhood and are now doing the same thing in India and the Far East… The Black man must awaken and claim his own.”_**

**_Restitution:_**

This refers to the restoration of something to its rightful owner. This includes freedom and rights, as well as property. Garvey believed that colonial authorities owed people of African descent a moral and historical debt. He said, **“_The white man has sinned against the black man for over four hundred years. He has deprived him of a knowledge of himself, he has robbed him of a country and has made him a slave, and then he has branded him as an inferior being. If the white man is honest, he will make the restitution that he can. If he is dishonest, then he must pay for it through the penalty of the Almighty God_.”**He asked for the return of what was robbed and exploited, including “our own civilization”.

**_Repatriation:_**

Thisgenerally refers to the return of something (or someone) to their country of origin. Garvey’s “Back to Africa” movement advocated for Black people in the diaspora to return to Africa and build an independent, powerful Black nation. Garvey said, **_“Our program is for the redemption of Africa. We are going to carry our people back home. We do not want to live among white men. We do not want to be subject to them. We want to build for ourselves. This is our chance to get a government, an empire of our own, and it is up to us to fight for that which is ours. We have given civilization to the world, and now they owe us a debt, and that debt will be collected.”_**

**_Economic self-sufficiency:_**

Garvey believed in **self-reliant****reparations****:** economic and institutional power through enterprises built by people of African descent. Garvey thus had economic empowerment as one of his aims towards the redemption of the Black race. Owning the means of production, and not just simply providing labour, was critical to black empowerment. At the heart of this economic scheme was also the formation of transnational economic linkages and of resource sharing within the race. Hence, there was the formation of a number of economic projects such as the Black Star Line, the Negro Factories Incorporated, the Negro World, The Black Man, and New Jamaican newspaper companies, the Edelweiss Amusement Company and other ventures.

However, Garvey still acknowledged that the colonial powers still **owed Black people access to capital and opportunity** after centuries of exploitation. Garvey said, **_“We are going to have our own businesses, our own ships, our own industries. That is what will repair the damage of slavery and injustice—not a gift from our oppressors, but power that we build ourselves. But the world owes us the chance and the capital to do it.”_**

Marcus Garvey was a strong advocate for racial justice and Black empowerment and made it clear that restitution must include land, freedom and control over one’s future. His philosophy and opinions not only support the reparations movement but formed the foundation of the cause.

## [Freedom’s Noble Cause](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/07/31/freedoms-noble-cause/)

Posted on [July 31, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/07/31/freedoms-noble-cause/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 6](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/aboliton.jpg?w=612)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/07/31/freedoms-noble-cause/)

In the English-speaking Caribbean, **Emancipation Day** is observed on **August 1 st**to commemorate the abolition of enslavement in the British Empire in 1834. This pivotal moment in Caribbean history not only signaled the legal end of enslavement but also represented the culmination of generations of resistance by enslaved Africans who fought tirelessly for their freedom. Today, Emancipation Day serves as a time of reflection on the atrocities of enslavement and the enduring resilience of the African diaspora.

Traditionally, Emancipation Day is marked with cultural festivals, ceremonies, church services, parades, and educational programmes. These activities shed light on the horrors of slavery, examine its lasting legacy, and honour the strength of those who endured and resisted. Another important way this legacy has been preserved is through the Arts including visual art, music, film, theatre, literature, and poetry. Each artistic medium plays a significant role in preserving and expressing the cultural memory of enslavement.

Poets, in particular, have long used poetry to reflect on the experience and legacy of enslavement. These poetic expressions often capture its emotional, political, and cultural dimensions. One such figure is the Rt. Excellent Marcus Mosiah Garvey, who employed poetry not only as a creative outlet but also as a tool for inspiration, political mobilization, and cultural reclamation. His poem _“Freedom’s Noble Cause, 1834–1934”_ commemorates the centenary of Emancipation while simultaneously issuing a revolutionary call to action.

**Freedom’s Noble Cause, 1834-1934**

**Behold the day, a cent’ry old,  
When fathers’ cares were lifted off:  
No more, as chattels to be sold,  
On block on farm, on ship or wharf.  
  
The sins of other men had made  
The world a living hell those days;  
But even as all sin do fade,  
The curse is gone, true freedom says.  
  
Profound regret we manifest  
That slavery brought us here:  
But God has done for us the best,  
And kept us in His kindly care.  
  
And now we rise as children new,  
To fight the battles fresh and keen:  
Our people, then, were sad and few,  
But now the millions can be seen.  
  
Good Buxton fought for us the fight  
With Knibbs, Wilberforce, Clarkson, too:  
They saw the awful, dreary night  
That shadowed us, of darkest hue.  
  
The hearts of England, called they out,  
Good Christian men, as they did prove:  
No stone unturned was left about,  
To ease us from the hellish grove.  
  
A century of histories  
Has brought us salving, trusting laws;  
And so we bless their memories,  
And sing for freedom’s noble cause.**

Garvey’s poem serves as both a tribute and a challenge. While it honours the sacrifices of abolitionists and the triumph of emancipation, it also reminds us that the journey toward full freedom is ongoing: “**And now we rise as children new, To fight the battles fresh and keen”**

## 2023 INDUCTEES

##### **Peggy Baker, O.Ont., C.M.**

Peggy Baker has been a vivid presence in contemporary dance for five decades, performing internationally with Lar Lubovitch, Mark Morris, Mikhail Baryshnikov, Doug Varone, Tere O’Connor, Molissa Fenley, and Charles Moulton (New York); Fortier Danse-Creation (Montreal); Toronto Dance Theatre, Dancemakers, and James Kudelka (Toronto). She established Peggy Baker Dance Projects in 1990, and for the first 20 years she dedicated herself to solo performance, winning rapturous praise for the eloquence and depth of her dancing and accolades for her collaborative partnerships with extraordinary choreographers, directors, musicians, and designers. Since 2010 she has focused on works for small ensemble and co-creation with solo dancers. Her work has been presented in art galleries, public spaces, and theatres across Canada and the U.S. (including Los Angeles, Jacob’s Pillow, and multiple venues in New York City), as well as Mexico, Argentina, Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, Korea, and Japan. Peggy’s many honours include The Order of Canada, the Walter Carsen Prize, the Premier’s Award, the Governor General’s Award, Honorary Doctorates from York University and the University of Calgary, and six Dora Mavor Moore Awards. She is the long-serving Artist-in-Residence at Canada’s National Ballet School and a fellow of the Bogliasco Foundation in Liguria, Italy.

##### ****Zab Maboungou****

Of French and Congolese origin, Zab Maboungou is the artistic director of Zab Maboungou/Compagnie Danse Nyata Nyata, a Montreal-based contemporary dance company founded in 1987. Her company’s artistic vocation encompasses creation, research, and teaching. Zab learned her craft in childhood through contact with traditional dance and music groups in Congo-Brazzaville, in the heady days of post-independence cultural effervescence. Since then, she has never stopped broadening her knowledge of the musical forms and dances of Africa. As a performer, she has integrated various traditional and “trad-modern” formations and ballets (from Central, West and East Africa). She co-directed and facilitated the first large-scale Pan-African French-language choreographic workshop in 1997. A philosophy teacher and author, Zab published _Heya Danse! Historique, poétique et didactique de la danse africaine_ in 2005. She is a sought-after speaker and a champion of diversity with a global understanding of the art of dance on and off stage. She has created more than 20 solo and group works in music and dance and is responsible for developing the LOKETO technique, drawing on the rhythmic foundations of African dances and musical forms. Zab has received numerous honours and awards internationally including the Governor General’s Award, being named Compagne de l’Ordre des arts et des lettres du Québec, and was honoured at the MASA, Marché des Arts du Spectacle d’Abidjan, Ivory Coast.

##### **Rex Harrington, O.C., F.R.S.C.**

One of the most accomplished and acclaimed male dancers of his era, Rex Harrington brought seemingly limitless panache, energy, style, and showmanship to the vast range of characterizations he created during his 20 years as a dancer with The National Ballet of Canada. Rex was born in Peterborough, Ontario, and graduated from Canada’s National Ballet School in 1981, joining The National Ballet of Canada in 1983. He became a Principal Dancer in 1988 and remained in that position until his retirement in 2004. A much sought-after dancer internationally, he performed with Teatro alla Scala, San Francisco Ballet, and Stuttgart Ballet. Renowned for his incomparable partnering skills, Rex danced with such legendary ballerinas as Ekaterina Maximova, Carla Fracci, Evelyn Hart, and Karen Kain. He created numerous roles during his career as a dancer, including the central role in James Kudelka’s _The Four Season_ s, Peter in Kudelka’s _The Nutcracker_, Lewis Carroll in Glen Tetley’s _Alice_, and The Young Gentleman in Tetley’s _La Ronde_, as well as lead roles in works by such choreographers as Jean-Pierre Perreault, Jiří Kylian, and Matjash Mrozewski. He was made an Officer of the Order of Canada in 2000 and was given a star on Canada’s Walk of Fame in 2005. In 2006, he was appointed Artist-in-Residence with the National Ballet and received an Honorary Degree from York University.
