##### **Karen Pheasant-Neganigwane**

Karen Pheasant-Neganigwane is an Anishinaabe of the Three Fires Confederacy (Ojibway, Odawa & Pottawatomi). She is a dancer, scholar, writer, artist, and orator from Wiikwemikoong, Manitoulin Island, Ontario. The daughter of residential school survivors, Karen’s path to activism and scholarly work started as a youth during the height of the civil rights era of the 1970s. The social project of Rochdale College (Toronto) provided the embryonic opening for her inquisitive spirit. Shortly after an engaging ceremony with a great Indigenous philosopher and scholar, Dr. Joe Couture, in the early 1980s, she left Toronto. She has spent the past 40 years being mentored by iconic Indigenous scholars from the Great Lakes of her people to Treaty Three, Treaty Six, and currently in Treaty Seven. Her Western education includes a B.A. in Political Science and English Literature, and graduate studies in Educational Policy Studies from the University of Alberta. She is completing a PhD in Educational Policy Studies/Indigenous Peoples Education with the University of Alberta. Karen is an Assistant Professor at Mount Royal University in the Treaty Seven region in the Department of General Education, Office of Teaching and Learning, and the Department of Humanities–Indigenous Studies. A life-long powwow dancer, Karen is the author of the award-winning book _Powwow: A Celebration Through Song and Dance_, which takes readers on a journey through powwow’s history and today’s thriving powwow culture.

##### **Edouard Lock, O.C., C.Q.**

Edouard Lock received international acclaim for his risky, virtuosic movement vocabulary. He began his choreographic career at the age of 20 and founded La La La Human Steps in 1980. He has created works for some of the world’s leading dance companies, including the Paris Opera Ballet, the Het Nationale Ballet of Holland, The Nederlands Dans Theater, the Cullberg Ballet, and the Royal Ballet of Flanders. He co-conceived and was artistic director for David Bowie’s world tour, _Sound and Vision_. He also collaborated with Frank Zappa on the Yellow Shark concerts. Various films have been made on Lock’s work including _Le Petit Musée de Vélasquez_ directed by Bernar Hébert, and the documentary _Inspirations_ by British director Michael Apted. The film adaptation of _Amelia_, directed by Edouard Lock, had its American premiere at the 2004 Tribeca Film Festival and its European premiere at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival. The film won its category at the Chicago International Film Festival, the Prague International Film Festival, and the Rose d’Or Festival in Switzerland, as well as winning two I.C.E. and two Gemini Awards for best direction and best editing.Edouard was named a Chevalier de l’Ordre National du Québec, is an Officer of the Order of Canada, and received a Governor General’s Award.

##### **Jean Stoneham Orr**

Jean Stoneham Orr was born in Edinburgh and came to Canada when she was still an infant. Her family settled in Saskatoon, which is where she started Highland dance. Her family moved to Vancouver when she was 9 years old and she began studying ballet. They moved to Ottawa during the Second World War and she continued her studies with Yolande Leduc and then Nesta Toumine. Jean was Canada’s first Giselle performing the role for the Ottawa Ballet Company in 1948 (directed by Leduc and Toumine). She danced with the Royal Winnipeg Ballet from 1951-1954. She married in 1954, which led to a hiatus with dance until she and her husband moved to Vancouver in 1971. Here, Jean became heavily involved in the Vancouver Ballet Society (VBS) as a volunteer. In the 1980s, she was the administrator for the VBS and played a substantial role in co-founding Ballet BC, for which she was also founding president of the board. Jean is still active as a volunteer in Vancouver’s ballet scene. She is a beloved member of the Vancouver dance community for her support of artists and her half-century of volunteerism.

## Community Builders Award

##### **Lawrence and Miriam Adams, C.M.**

The Adamses were active as performers, teachers, choreographers, dissidents, archivists, publishers, and founders of Dance Collection Danse (DCD). St. Boniface, Manitoba-born Lawrence was renowned for his riveting National Ballet of Canada (NBoC) performances as Mercutio in John Cranko’s _Romeo and Juliet_. Miriam, born and raised in Toronto, was a graduate of Canada’s National Ballet School (NBS) and joined NBoC in 1963. Following their departure, they formed the group “15 Dancers” with their students in 1972, and converted a downtown Toronto space into a theatre in 1974. Miriam’s choreographic work embraced satire, while Lawrence’s explored the scientific and aesthetic impact of the brick. After presenting Miriam’s _Another Nutcracker_, they re-established the theatre as 15 Dance Laboratorium – welcoming dance artists from across the country. They published the newspapers _SPILL_ and _Canadian Dance News_; and to enliven interest in dance history, recorded interviews with Canada’s dance pioneers. These initiatives piloted ENCORE! ENCORE! to reconstruct and notate mid-20th-century Canadian choreographies … leading to the creation of DCD, Canada’s dance archives/museum, and publisher of 41 books. Miriam’s honours include the Toronto Arts Foundation’s Rita Davies and Margo Bindhardt Cultural Leadership Award, Member of the Order of Canada, and the Ken McCarter Award for Distinguished NBS Alumni. Lawrence passed away in 2003. He is remembered as a charismatic performer, mentor, leader, catalyst for change, and a larger-than-life personality.

##### **Mimi Beck**

Mimi Beck has dedicated her career to advancing and promoting dance in all forms. ## Trailblazers

##### **Irene Apinée and Jury Gotshalks, Grace Tinning, Don Gillies**

**Irene Apinée and Jury Gotshalks** were dancers with the Latvian Opera Ballet in Riga prior to the Second World War. After the Russian invasion of Latvia, Jury was forced into slave labour and the two were separated. They found each other at the end of the war in a displaced persons camp in western Germany. With other displaced artists, they created the Latvian Exile Ballet touring displaced persons camps, performing for cigarettes and other items that they could trade for food and materials. Irene used the same pointe shoes for two years. They starched gauze with potato water to make tutus and used parachute silk for other costumes. In 1948, the Gotshalks and their young son were sponsored by the Halifax Music Conservatory to immigrate to Canada and set up a ballet school in Halifax. By 1950, they had trained a core group of senior students to perform with them at the 1950 Canadian Ballet Festival as the Gotshalks Halifax Ballet. In 1951, Jury and Irene became charter members of the National Ballet of Canada while they also juggled operating their company from afar for another season. They also danced on CBC television and with Les Grands Ballets Canadiens in the 1960s.

**Grace Tinning** – was the social pages editor of the _Regina Leader-Post_ in the 1930s. She had graduated from Rupert’s Land College in Winnipeg and had also passed her solo performer and piano teacher examinations at the Toronto Conservatory of Music. Her early dance training was with Dorothy Rowell in Regina and then later at the Mary Wigman School in New York. It is likely that her Eurhythmics training came from the Toronto Conservatory of Music, where Madeleine Boss Lasserre taught Eurhythmics. Tinning was one of the first movement instructors at the Banff School of Fine Arts teaching in 1936 and 1937, and possibly as early as 1935. In Regina, she led a dance group focussed on expressive movement and Eurhythmics, embracing the foundations of movement developed by the forerunners of modern dance such as Isadora Duncan. She was also involved in the Regina Little Theatre Society in the 1930s.

**Don Gillies** trained with Boris Volkoff in the 1940s and danced in the Volkoff Canadian Ballet at several of the Canadian Ballet Festivals. In the early 1950s he went to England on a scholarship from the Volkoff company to train further and eventually earned a position in the Sadler’s Wells Junior Ballet. He also began to choreograph at this time, staging his work independently in London, where he also performed in Gene Kelly’s film _Invitation to the Dance_. He returned to Canada in the mid-1950s and began to choreograph for Janet Baldwin’s company for the Canadian Ballet Festivals. In the 1960s, he was an acclaimed choreographer and performer for CBC television, primarily for _The Wayne and Shuster Show_. In the 1970s and ’80s, he did considerable work choreographing musicals in Ontario and Nova Scotia for both professional and amateur productions, and eventually settled in Nova Scotia where he was a notable teacher of master classes for Dance Nova Scotia.

## [Garvey’s views on Obeah/Superstition](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/)

Posted on [April 30, 2026](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/obeah.jpg?w=168)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2026/04/30/garveys-views-on-obeah-superstition/)

While sorting through the Garvey Research/Reference Library’s collection recently, a research document was discovered that made reference to Garvey being suspected of practising Obeah. Olive Senior’s Encyclopedia of Jamaican Heritage defines obeah as being, “**_The word used in Jamaica to denote witchcraft, evil magic or sorcery by which supernatural power is invoked to achieve personal protection or the destruction of enemies_**”. The document identified stated that Garvey had erected a statue of an African Queen on the property of his Jamaican residence, Somali Court, which raised suspicion. In an apparent move to break Garvey’s occult practices, the statue was stolen and found destroyed days later.

Why the assumption that Garvey was delving into the supernatural, though? Could it be because of his mystique or his perceived omnipotence? In his presentation as guest speaker at the 2014 staging of the Annual Marcus Mosiah Garvey Lecture at Liberty Hall: The Legacy of Marcus Garvey, Prof. Robert Hill, renowned Garvey scholar, hypothesized that Garvey was accompanied by a fallen angel which contributed to his supposed magical and mystical powers. The idea that Marcus Garvey was involved in witchcraft or the supernatural seems to have been a persistent rumour perpetuated by his critics. One can only imagine that this was done in order to undermine his credibility.

These claims of Garvey indulging in obeah/witchcraft are unfounded. Based on his speeches and writings, it is obvious that Garvey held obeah in low regard. He grouped obeah with superstition and viewed them as backward practices. For instance, in a speech Garvey delivered at Edelweiss Park on July 10, 1932, titled, “**The new Jamaica and how we can build it**”, he said “**_Stop making obeah to be our national contribution; because this does your country no good, and anything that does not benefit your country will not benefit you_**”. Prior to this statement, in the same speech, he had said, “**_Your only production is the bananas and cocoanuts and these are not man-made, they are the creation of God; but everything resulting from the genius of man that shows the character of man you are without; you have nothing typical to show except obeah (laughter) and that has no effect_**”. In a report on Garvey by Inspector W.A. Orrett of the Falmouth Constabulary Office, dated March 14, 1928, Garvey was quoted as saying, “**_Black man goes to the obeah man to keep down his fellowman. Set duppy to give him big foot_**”.

Marcus Garvey generally spoke about **obeah/superstition**in a way that was **critical, dismissive and sometimes humourous.**He essentially treated obeah as something that could undermine racial upliftment efforts and distract from economic and political growth. However, his criticism of obeah should not be seen as a rejection of African heritage as he strongly promoted African identity and Black pride.

## [JAMAICAN-BASED DANCERS IN THE UNIA](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/)

Posted on [November 3, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 3](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/sagwa-bennett.jpg?w=444)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/)

Marcus Garvey was a cultured man who used the Arts to empower Black people and build their character. He achieved this through the activities of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Cultural units were established in the performing arts and members of these units were given a salary.

Dance was one aspect of the Arts that the UNIA paid particular attention to. It played a significant role in the UNIA. It served not only as a means of entertainment, but also as a tool for cultural pride, unity and resistance. Dances and dance competitions were often held at Edelweiss Park and the Kingston Liberty Hall and they were used to liberate black people.

Garvey launched and/or supported the careers of several Jamaican-based dancers. Many of Jamaica’s top show dancers came out of the UNIA’s cultural units. These included Harold ‘**_Kid Harold_**’ Smith, Randolph ‘**_Ranny_**’ Williams and Arthur ‘**_Sagwa_**’ Bennett. The dance group, **_The Follies_**, was also a popular unit out of the UNIA.

**Harold ‘_Kid Harold’_ Smith**

Kid Harold was a prominent Jamaican tap dancer who was also a part of the comedy duo ‘**Harold and Trim’**. He was affiliated with the UNIA’s cultural programme at Edelweiss Park and he led a dance group called Butterfly Troupe. At Edelweiss Park he also trained aspiring dancers and sometimes served as a judge for the dancing contests hosted by the UNIA. Kid Harold had said that Garvey’s legacy in the field of dance was to provide some of the best professional dancers on the entertainment circuit.

**Randolph ‘_Ranny_’ Williams**

Ranny Williams is popularly known as an actor and comedian. However, he began his career as a dancer in the UNIA. He was first a backline dancer, then a frontline dancer and eventually a feature dancer with partners. Ranny was described as a good dancer and became a popular feature of the UNIA’s entertainment programmes.

**Arthur ‘_Sagwa_’ Bennett**

Sagwa Bennett was a dancer/performer with the UNIA who also worked as a dance trainer for a dance troupe. He appeared in many of the musical comedies produced by Ranny Williams.

**The Follies**

The most popular cultural unit of the UNIA was a dance group named the Follies. This was a group of dancers who performed choreographed Broadway-style pieces that incorporated mento-style movements. The Follies often performed in cabaret shows, musical revues and concerts. They also usually performed every Monday night at Edelweiss Park and at the monthly concerts there

## [Garvey supports reparations](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/08/29/garvey-supports-reparations/)

Posted on [August 29, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/08/29/garvey-supports-reparations/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 4](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/reparations.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/08/29/garvey-supports-reparations/)

The International Center for Transitional Justice (ICTJ) defines reparations as “… **_to acknowledge and repair the causes and consequences of human rights violations and nequality in countries emerging from dictatorship, armed conflict and political violence, as well as in societies dealing with racial injustice and legacies of colonization._**” Though Marcus Garvey did not use the actual term “**_reparations_**”, he was a strong advocate for restitution to people of African descent. He believed that this could be achieved through African redemption, racial solidarity and racial self reliance. Consequently, some of his tenets align with some of the principles of reparations.

**_Anti-Colonialism:_**

Garvey spoke and wrote extensively on the exploitative and undemocratic nature of colonialism, which included among other things, the political subjugation of the masses, economic exploitation, and racial segregation. He not only opposed colonialism in Africa and the Caribbean, but also its existence everywhere. He supported the nationalist movements in China, India, and the Eastern European states. Garvey said, **_“The British, the French, the Dutch, and others have raped Africa of her manhood and are now doing the same thing in India and the Far East… The Black man must awaken and claim his own.”_**

**_Restitution:_**

This refers to the restoration of something to its rightful owner. This includes freedom and rights, as well as property. Garvey believed that colonial authorities owed people of African descent a moral and historical debt. He said, **“_The white man has sinned against the black man for over four hundred years. He has deprived him of a knowledge of himself, he has robbed him of a country and has made him a slave, and then he has branded him as an inferior being. If the white man is honest, he will make the restitution that he can. If he is dishonest, then he must pay for it through the penalty of the Almighty God_.”**He asked for the return of what was robbed and exploited, including “our own civilization”.

**_Repatriation:_**

Thisgenerally refers to the return of something (or someone) to their country of origin. Garvey’s “Back to Africa” movement advocated for Black people in the diaspora to return to Africa and build an independent, powerful Black nation. Garvey said, **_“Our program is for the redemption of Africa. We are going to carry our people back home. We do not want to live among white men. We do not want to be subject to them. We want to build for ourselves. This is our chance to get a government, an empire of our own, and it is up to us to fight for that which is ours. We have given civilization to the world, and now they owe us a debt, and that debt will be collected.”_**

**_Economic self-sufficiency:_**

Garvey believed in **self-reliant****reparations****:** economic and institutional power through enterprises built by people of African descent. Garvey thus had economic empowerment as one of his aims towards the redemption of the Black race. Owning the means of production, and not just simply providing labour, was critical to black empowerment. At the heart of this economic scheme was also the formation of transnational economic linkages and of resource sharing within the race. Hence, there was the formation of a number of economic projects such as the Black Star Line, the Negro Factories Incorporated, the Negro World, The Black Man, and New Jamaican newspaper companies, the Edelweiss Amusement Company and other ventures.

However, Garvey still acknowledged that the colonial powers still **owed Black people access to capital and opportunity** after centuries of exploitation. Garvey said, **_“We are going to have our own businesses, our own ships, our own industries. That is what will repair the damage of slavery and injustice—not a gift from our oppressors, but power that we build ourselves. But the world owes us the chance and the capital to do it.”_**

Marcus Garvey was a strong advocate for racial justice and Black empowerment and made it clear that restitution must include land, freedom and control over one’s future. His philosophy and opinions not only support the reparations movement but formed the foundation of the cause.

## [One “Black” Church?](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/01/31/one-black-church/)

Posted on [January 31, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/01/31/one-black-church/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 5](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/black-church-feature.jpg?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/01/31/one-black-church/)

The Right Excellent Marcus Garvey was a spiritual man; in fact, he was Christian. He recognized that there is a God and that we should believe in Him. Despite his changing denominations throughout his lifetime, (from Methodist to Catholic) God remained a central, influential figure in Garvey’s life. In his poem, “**_The Everlasting Life_**”, the third verse says:

“**_It’s safer then to have one God_**

**_Whose life is first and ever so_**

**_And all the rest to live in Him_**

**_With all the good they ever had_** …”

Though religion played an important part of the work of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (U.N.I.A), it is important to note that Garvey never intended for the U.N.I.A to be a church nor did he intend for the U.N.I.A to adopt a church. In the editorial of the July 17, 1921 issue of the Negro World with headline, “**_U.N.I.A Favors All Churches, But Adopts None as U.N.I.A Church_**” it stated, “**_the U.N.I.A is not a church, and does not intend to be one. So far as the present signs are, there will be no church connected with the U.N.I.A.”_**However, this view did not negate Garvey’s belief that, “**_The Church is the most beneficent institution, the greatest civilizing agency;_**”

Garvey encouraged an African interpretation of Christianity, which dispelled the white/European interpretation of God being white. He saw the need to make religion relevant to the Black experience. Circa 1919, he met an aspiring priest named George Alexander McGuire who shared his views on black theology. Consequently, he appointed him as Chaplain-General for the U.N.I.A. However, whilst it seemed as if McGuire wanted the U.N.I.A to adopt the African Orthodox Church (AOC) as the official church of the U.N.I.A, Garvey, on the other hand, though he endorsed the idea of a “Black Church”, did not want to alienate anyone because of their religious belief. So, the AOC was never adopted by the U.N.I.A. though it was formed by clergy in the movement. Eventually, McGuire broke away from the U.N.I.A to focus on the development of the AOC that he founded in 1921.

Garvey’s resistance to having the U.N.I.A devoted to one Church was that it would cause division among the members. With practitioners of the many different denominations and faiths existing in the U.N.I.A, Garvey thought that forcing all the members to follow one religious doctrine would be disruptive to the movement. He recognized that religion could be a divisive force and as such, he tried to promote unity and support all faiths that promoted “Black” theology.

## [MARCUS GARVEY AND AMY ASHWOOD: A UNION OF LOVE AND ACTIVISM](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/12/23/marcus-garvey-and-amy-ashwood-a-union-of-love-and-activism/)

Posted on [December 23, 2024 February 12, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/12/23/marcus-garvey-and-amy-ashwood-a-union-of-love-and-activism/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 6](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/image.png?w=648)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/12/23/marcus-garvey-and-amy-ashwood-a-union-of-love-and-activism/)

On December 25, 1919, Marcus Mosiah Garvey, the charismatic leader of the Universal Negro Improvement Association and African Communities League (UNIA/ACL), married Amy Ashwood, a fellow activist and trailblazer in the early Pan-African movement. Their wedding, held at Liberty Hall in Harlem, New York, symbolized more than a personal commitment—it marked a powerful partnership in the shared struggle for African empowerment.

The ceremony, attended by allies and members of the UNIA, was a celebration of African heritage and the Pan-African ideals that both Garvey and Ashwood championed. Liberty Hall, a significant site for Garveyism and Black empowerment, was a fitting venue for this historic event. Their union reflected the merging of two passionate advocates dedicated to the liberation and upliftment of people of African descent.

**Visionaries in the fight for freedom**

Marcus Garvey, renowned for his pioneering work in Black Nationalism, envisioned a global movement where people of African descent could unite, reclaim their dignity, and achieve economic independence. Through initiatives like the Black Star Line and his iconic slogan, _“Africa for the Africans,”_ he inspired millions across the diaspora. His tireless efforts were fueled by a belief in self-reliance and the reclamation of cultural pride.

Amy Ashwood, equally formidable, was a staunch advocate for women’s rights and social justice. Born into a prominent Afro-Jamaican family, she was a founding member of the UNIA and a vocal supporter of Pan-Africanism. Ashwood’s advocacy extended beyond the political sphere to embrace education and cultural enrichment. Reflecting on her role, she once said, _“Women must be the guardians of our future, nurturing the seeds of knowledge and unity for generations to come.”_

**Challenges in Revolutionary Relationships**

Despite the promise of their union, the marriage faced significant personal and political challenges. Garvey’s unrelenting dedication to his work often kept him away, causing tensions between the couple. By 1922 their marriage had ended, but their shared mission endured. Garvey later married Amy Jacques, another influential UNIA figure, while Ashwood continued her activism independently.

Ashwood’s subsequent work, including the establishment of the International African Friends of Ethiopia, exemplified her unwavering commitment to African independence and unity. This period underscores how personal sacrifices often intertwine with the demands of revolutionary movements.

**A Legacy that endures**

Marcus Garvey and Amy Ashwood remain icons of the Black liberation struggle. Their wedding, held on Christmas Day at Liberty Hall, stands as a significant moment in the history of the Pan-African movement. It symbolizes the intersection of love, activism, and a vision for a better world.

Their work laid the foundation for much of the Pan-Africanist movement that continues to inspire generations. As Garvey famously said, _“A people without the knowledge of their past history, origin, and culture is like a tree without roots.”_ Their shared efforts ensured that future generations would remain deeply rooted in their heritage.

**Reflection and call to action**

The story of Marcus Garvey and Amy Ashwood invites us to reflect on the power of unity, resilience, and shared purpose in the face of adversity. How can we draw inspiration from their legacy to address today’s struggles for justice, equality, and empowerment? Let us honor their contributions by continuing to uplift and unite our communities.

## [BLACK WOMEN OF VALOUR: Amy Jacques Garvey (1895-1973)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/11/25/black-women-of-valour-amy-jacques-garvey-1895-1973/)

Posted on [November 25, 2024](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/11/25/black-women-of-valour-amy-jacques-garvey-1895-1973/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 7](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/garvey-amy-jacques-portrait.jpg?w=200)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/11/25/black-women-of-valour-amy-jacques-garvey-1895-1973/)

“But you have been a light to me,  
A fond and dear, and true Amie;  
So what care I for falsest friend,  
When on your love I can depend.”

– **_Marcus Garvey_**

Amy Euphemia Jacques Garvey was an Author, Pan-Africanist, Journalist, Black Nationalist and the second wife of the Right Excellent Marcus Mosiah Garvey. Born to middle class parents, George Samuel Jacques and Charlotte Henrietta Jacques, in Kingston, Jamaica, on December 31, 1895, Jacques attended St. Patrick’s School, Deaconess High School (_now St. Hugh’s High_) and Wolmer’s High School for Girls. After graduating high school, she worked for some time, then later migrated to the United States in 1917. There she became involved in the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA) after hearing Garvey speak at a gathering in Harlem. Garvey was so impressed by the ideas she presented to him that he offered her a job.

Much of what is known about Marcus Garvey is as a result of the efforts of Amy Jacques. Having been his personal secretary, travelling companion, the office manager at UNIA headquarters and secretary of the Negro Factories Corporation, confidante, and then eventually his wife, Amy Jacques knew Garvey intimately and was perfectly positioned to collate material for, and edit the popular **Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey,**published in 1923, as well as author the book, **Garvey & Garveyism,**published in 1963. She also gave speeches and published editorials, using these media to empower Black women and encourage them to join the UNIA.She also collated two collections of essays, “**Black Power in America**” and “**The Impact of Garvey in Africa and Jamaica**“.

When Garvey went to prison in Atlanta, Amy Jacques became his principal lieutenant from 1925 to 1927. She single-handedly marketed the two volumes of **Philosophy and Opinions of Marcus Garvey** in order to raise funds for Garvey’s legal defense.After Garvey’s death in 1940, Jacques became a contributing editor to a Black Nationalist journal, **The African**, published in Harlem in the 1940s, and established the African Study Circle of the World in Jamaica in the late 1940s. She died on July 25, 1973 and is buried in the St. Andrew Parish Church Cemetery.

Amy Jacques is the mother of Garvey’s two sons, Marcus Mosiah Garvey Jr. (_now deceased_), and Dr. Julius Winston Garvey, born in 1930 and 1933 respectively.

In recognition of her contribution to the pan-African and feminist movements, Amy Jacques Garvey was awarded the Gold Musgrave Medal in 1971. In that same year, the then College of Arts, Science and Technology (C.A.S.T) built the Amy Jacques Hall, a dormitory complex exclusively for women. The community centre on Jacques Road, Mountain View was also recently renovated and renamed the Amy Jacques Garvey Community Centre on her birthday in 2022, to honour the woman who once lived in the community. In fact, her family owned much of the land in the area which is why Jacques Road was so named.

As we celebrate Amy Jacques Garvey’s 129th birthday on December 31st, let us remember her not just as the second wife of Marcus Garvey, but as a true, lifelong champion for racial and gender equality and rights.

## [The importance of Education to Garvey](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/10/30/the-importance-of-education-to-garvey/)

Posted on [October 30, 2024](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/10/30/the-importance-of-education-to-garvey/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 8](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/garvey-marcus-in-academic-attire.jpg?w=300)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/10/30/the-importance-of-education-to-garvey/)

Marcus Garvey was an avid advocate for education. In fact, Education was one of his priorities. He said “**_Education is the medium by which a people are prepared for the creation of their own particular civilization and the advancement and glory of their own race._**” He also said that, “**_It is by education that we become prepared for our duties and responsibilities in life._**

Education was a critical point in the manifesto of the People’s Political Party, formed by Garvey. The manifesto called for vocational and skills training schools in each of the three counties of Jamaica; a high school in every parish, a polytechnic, and a university. Garvey’s vision of establishing such institutions was borne out of his being inspired by the Tuskegee University in Alabama founded by African-American, Booker T. Washington. The philosophy of self-sufficiency and social segregation embodied in the Tuskegee curriculum, were inspirations to Garvey.

Why was education so important to Garvey? He knew that education was a method by which Black people could improve their lives and build their nations. He also believed that education was critical to nation-building. Garvey said that Blacks needed to make their education practical and real in order to be responsible citizens. For example, he believed that Black people should be self-sufficient and become entrepreneurs and, that the only way to accomplish this is through education. However, he felt that Black people were at a disadvantage in the educational system then, as it was tailored to favour the White race as a means to control Blacks. It does not seem as if much has changed.

It is said that children who do not complete basic education naturally grow to become adults without proper civic, social and cultural contact, hence their behaviour as adults become more criminal. This then greatly affects the expense of criminal administration, which is approximately three times the expense of educational administration. So, it is evident that it is best for a nation to educate the population. The teachings and philosophy of National Hero, Marcus Garvey, with a special emphasis on education, could go a long way in helping to reduce crime and addressing some of Jamaica’s other social ills.

Each of us could improve our lives and build our nation by building our self esteem and that of our children and pointing them in the direction of education. We also need to re-instill excellence in our children, and the fact that they can achieve excellence; Garvey stood for excellence. One way to do this is to encourage excellence through the provision of grants, scholarships and awards to persons who excel in their studies or show potential. Diligence should always be awarded.

Garvey’s own life, work and accomplishments are testimony to the possibilities for rising above any obstacle to accomplish greatness. They also provide many important lessons for personal development and nation-building.

## [Who was the “Bread King”?](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/09/30/who-was-the-bread-king/)

Posted on [September 30, 2024](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/09/30/who-was-the-bread-king/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 9](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/amos-shackleford.jpg?w=142)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2024/09/30/who-was-the-bread-king/)

The name Amos Shackleford may not be commonly known in Jamaica, however, in Nigeria the name was synonymous to success. In the early 1900s, Shackleford was one of few Jamaicans who embraced Marcus Garvey’s vision for Blacks to return to Africa and help to develop the continent through a successful enterprise – a bakery.

Besides sharing the vision of returning to Africa, Amos Stanley Wynter Shackleford and Marcus Mosiah Garvey seemed to have shared other similarities, throughout their lives. Firstly, both were born in 1887, Shackleford in January and Garvey in August. They both came from humble backgrounds with both their fathers being tradesmen; Shackleford’s father was a saddle-maker and Garvey’s was a stonemason. Both men started working at early ages; Shackleford began working with the Jamaican railway at age 16 years, while Garvey began working as a printing apprentice at age 14 years. Shackleford and Garvey both migrated from Jamaica; Shackleford headed to Nigeria, Africa and Garvey headed to New York, U.S.A. In 1920, Shackleford founded the Lagos branch of the UNIA-ACL, the organization founded by Garvey in 1914, and became President. Later on he, along with Herbert Macaulay, the father of Nigerian nationalism, founded the first major Nigerian political party, the Nigerian National Democratic Party (NNDP). Similarly, Marcus Garvey founded Jamaica’s first modern political party, the People’s Political Party in 1929 (PPP).

Of course, there were significant differences between the two. One such difference was the fact that unlike Shackleford, Garvey never got to see his vision to go “back to Africa” materialize as he never got the opportunity to go to Africa. Another way in which the men differed was their focus within the UNIA. Shackleford concentrated on the social, industrial and commercial programmes within the UNIA and neglected to promote the political aspect of the organization’s programme.

No doubt, Garvey would have been proud of Shackleford’s accomplishments in Nigeria; he was another Black man’s success story. After leaving the railway service, Shackleford, along with his wife, established what was to become a very successful enterprise. He revolutionized the local bread industry in Nigeria by introducing major innovations and marketing techniques over the years that greatly improved efficiency and product quality. His business grew significantly and even expanded to Ghana. Shackleford’s bakeries and breads became so popular that he earned the title “**_Bread King_**” and the breads were called “**_Shacklefords_**”.

Shackleford was also actively involved in Nigerian politics. After co-founding the NNDP, he served as Vice-President and eventually President after Macaulay’s death in 1946; a post he held until his passing. Shackleford also sat on the Lagos Town Council from 1929 to 1938.

Though Amos Shackleford was “bread royalty” in Nigeria, he never severed ties with his homeland, Jamaica. He sent his sons back to Jamaica to be schooled and when he remarried, he and his wife, Gwendolyn James, purchased a house at the corner of Old Hope Road and Retreat Avenue in St. Andrew which they called “**_Shalimar_**”. Though they resided mainly in Nigeria, the couple made their Jamaica home available to their Jamaican “friends”. In fact, a few weeks before Mr. Shackleford’s passing on December 31, 1954, Mr. And Mrs. Norman and Edna Manley held their Christmas Party there on December 11.

When Shackleford fell ill in 1950, he and his wife returned to Jamaica for a holiday, however, this was the last time Shackleford would see his native homeland. He regarded himself as a Nigerian, having lived there for most of his life. So, he was buried in Lagos, at his request.

Amos Shackleford made significant contributions to both Jamaica and Nigeria and as such, was deservedly listed in the Who’s Who in Jamaica 1941-1946 and the Nigerian Who’s Who for 1934.

## [JAMAICAN-BASED DANCERS IN THE UNIA](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/)

Posted on [November 3, 2025](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/) by [garveylhkgn](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/author/garveylhkgn/)

[![Image 2](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/sagwa-bennett.jpg?w=444)](https://garveylhkgn.wordpress.com/2025/11/03/jamaican-based-dancers-in-the-unia/)

Marcus Garvey was a cultured man who used the Arts to empower Black people and build their character. He achieved this through the activities of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA). Cultural units were established in the performing arts and members of these units were given a salary.

Dance was one aspect of the Arts that the UNIA paid particular attention to. It played a significant role in the UNIA. It served not only as a means of entertainment, but also as a tool for cultural pride, unity and resistance. Dances and dance competitions were often held at Edelweiss Park and the Kingston Liberty Hall and they were used to liberate black people.

Garvey launched and/or supported the careers of several Jamaican-based dancers. Many of Jamaica’s top show dancers came out of the UNIA’s cultural units. These included Harold ‘**_Kid Harold_**’ Smith, Randolph ‘**_Ranny_**’ Williams and Arthur ‘**_Sagwa_**’ Bennett. The dance group, **_The Follies_**, was also a popular unit out of the UNIA.

**Harold ‘_Kid Harold’_ Smith**

Kid Harold was a prominent Jamaican tap dancer who was also a part of the comedy duo ‘**Harold and Trim’**. He was affiliated with the UNIA’s cultural programme at Edelweiss Park and he led a dance group called Butterfly Troupe. At Edelweiss Park he also trained aspiring dancers and sometimes served as a judge for the dancing contests hosted by the UNIA. Kid Harold had said that Garvey’s legacy in the field of dance was to provide some of the best professional dancers on the entertainment circuit.

**Randolph ‘_Ranny_’ Williams**

Ranny Williams is popularly known as an actor and comedian. However, he began his career as a dancer in the UNIA. He was first a backline dancer, then a frontline dancer and eventually a feature dancer with partners. Ranny was described as a good dancer and became a popular feature of the UNIA’s entertainment programmes.

**Arthur ‘_Sagwa_’ Bennett**

Sagwa Bennett was a dancer/performer with the UNIA who also worked as a dance trainer for a dance troupe. He appeared in many of the musical comedies produced by Ranny Williams.

**The Follies**

The most popular cultural unit of the UNIA was a dance group named the Follies. This was a group of dancers who performed choreographed Broadway-style pieces that incorporated mento-style movements. The Follies often performed in cabaret shows, musical revues and concerts. They also usually performed every Monday night at Edelweiss Park and at the monthly concerts there

Title: Miriam Landis | Ballet & Books on Instagram: "I used to be a professional ballerina with Miami City Ballet, but I gave it all up. 

I grew up in Utah and was a ballet student at the Ballet West Academy.

At age 16, I moved to New York to attend the School of American Ballet. 

My dream was to join New York City Ballet. 

I was devastated when they told me no, but my ballet journey wasn’t over. 

I was offered a position at MCB, where I danced roles like the Flower Festival in Genzano pas de deux, the Steadfast Tin Soldier, Scotch Girl in Scotch Symphony, and the Liberty Bell in Stars and Stripes. 

However, the ballet world was draining on me. 

I decided to give it all up. 

I ended up going to Stanford and worked in book publishing. 

Eventually, I moved to Seattle for a job on the Amazon Books team. 

But I couldn’t fully leave ballet behind, 

so I started teaching again, 

became a ballet mom, 

and wrote three ballet books that sold over 10,000 copies. 

My ballet journey has changed over the years, and it’s still evolving. 

Follow me to see what’s next.

#laureninthelimelight #girlinmotion #girlonpointe"

But I couldn’t fully leave ballet behind,   
  
so I started teaching again,   
  
became a ballet mom,   
  
and wrote three ballet books that sold over 10,000 copies.   
  
My ballet journey has changed over the years, and it’s still evolving.

I used to be a professional ballerina with Miami City Ballet, but I gave it all up.   
  
I grew up in Utah and was a ballet student at the Ballet West Academy.  
  
At age 16, I moved to New York to attend the School of American Ballet.   
  
My dream was to join New York City Ballet.   
  
I was devastated when they told me no, but my ballet journey wasn’t over.   
  
I was offered a position at MCB, where I danced roles like the Flower Festival in Genzano pas de deux, the Steadfast Tin Soldier, Scotch Girl in Scotch Symphony, and the Liberty Bell in Stars and Stripes.   
  
However, the ballet world was draining on me.   
  
I decided to give it all up.   
  
I ended up going to Stanford and worked in book publishing.   
  
Eventually, I moved to Seattle for a job on the Amazon Books team.   
  
But I couldn’t fully leave ballet behind,   
  
so I started teaching again,   
  
became a ballet mom,   
  
and wrote three ballet books that sold over 10,000 copies.   
  
My ballet journey has changed over the years, and it’s still evolving.   
  
Follow me to see what’s next.

And this one happened this past summer at Birthday Celebration at the Cabin.  It was extremely hot and there was no ac where we were having the party across the river.  I was concerned about the heat for everyone and mostly mom.  I literally 5 minutes before this stood in front of the cabin as a friend saw and prayed to God to pleaseeeee cool down the weather.  This happened 5 minutes later 😳. Sometimes all we have to do is ask.  Keep asking.  Keep praying.  Happy Sunday. Go Rest 💗🙏🏽 🗣️ @poohbearjen"

[![Image 19: Flannery O’Connor Award winner Toni Ann Johnson was at Baltimore’s @redemmas in conversation with @khadijahonline for the release of her new collection of linked short stories, which explores the sometimes painful and often humorous experiences of the Arringtons as an upper-middle-class Black family in a predominantly white, working-class community. It’s 1963 in the small town of Monroe, New York. The Arringtons, a Black family, buy a house in a picturesque, all-white neighborhood. Some residents are welcoming, but many react to Dr. Philip Arrington, his wife Velma, and their daughters Livia and Maddie by conspiring against their success in both big and small ways. Amid this mix of hostility and shaky acceptance, the Arringtons must navigate their careers, deal with a volatile marriage, and raise their daughters. This book follows Johnson’s previous collection, Light Skin Gone to Waste, which won the 2021 Flannery O’Connor Award. Through multiple perspectives and moments in time, from the 1960s to 2022, readers are invited into the lives of the eldest daughter, who longs for her father’s affection while striving for independence; the youngest daughter, who seeks to overcome childhood pain through music and love; a father practicing psychology while engaging in affairs with the white women of the town; and a mother dealing with infidelity while raising her daughters in a place that rejects them. Deeply emotional, funny, and unflinchingly honest, But Where’s Home? lays bare the realities of Black life in America, challenging readers to confront racism, classism, colonized thinking, narcissism, abuse, and troubled parent-child relationships. Reconciliation and Self Forgiveness.

Youth Sunday at TNECC: Choose Life.

Since age to my perception was corrupted by the way the mind is designed to survive life.

Transition and Change for some people are emotional fractures. 

There is a natural break in communication between the child and the role of a father and child and role of a mother.

We are born in rebellion and shaped in iniquity. 

Shame, Embarrassment and Disappointment can’t be avoided and we can teach skills how to manage transitions and change in our perception of life early on in age.

#percepcion #life #kingdomcitizen #emotionalintelligence #mindset"

I stated that we need to”Builders” often times.  And I stand by that statement.

I’m aware of all the complexities that come alongside that.  Trust me.

A lot of you reached out in my DM’s and text to further this conversation.  I spoke with some voices I trust and wanted to give some insight into a few things Younger Individuals may be looking for.

This isn’t exhaustive, and to be clear, I’m in the process of practicing a lot of this in my own context. 

If you deem yourself a “young adult”…give some more recommendations in the comments please.  Let’s help everyone out here 

Live in Purpose…On Purpose"

Title: Farron🪖 on Instagram: "So as I waited my turn… 

I was in my head about what I have been at War with in my life that I still pretend sometimes like I’m ok..

So I did a doubting Thomas or I would say I was talking to God.. saying to myself.. God I don’t just not trust people or myself.. I don’t completely trust you.. 

So I had lack of trust in my spirit as I self examined my subconscious mind..

I told God if you know my heart  Lord and if you really do know my heart then you tell me what’s in my thoughts..

And this was the results… 

He ran down my whole laundry list.. 

Rejection, Fear, Insecurit, Anxiety. 

I’ve been able to recognize these and manage them but still only in my will not God’s Will.. 

I’m at War with myself… This is why I said people are not your problem. 

All tied to a story that my subconscious mind has collected the first 40 years of my life that has proof that I tell myself moreso live from this belief tha lt “I’m not worth it”

[![Image 17: Good morning tune goons my girlfriend is actually on a trip in California right now so I thought this song fits my present situation Led Zeppelin were an English rock band formed in London in 1968. The band comprised vocalist Robert Plant, guitarist Jimmy Page, bassist-keyboardist John Paul Jones and drummer John Bonham. With a heavy, guitar-driven sound and drawing from influences including blues and folk music, Led Zeppelin are cited as a progenitor of hard rock and heavy metal. Among the best-selling music artists of all time, they influenced the music industry, particularly in the development of album-oriented rock and stadium rock.Led Zeppelin evolved from a previous band, the Yardbirds, and were originally named “the New Yardbirds”. They signed a deal with Atlantic Records that gave them considerable artistic freedom. Initially unpopular with critics, they achieved commercial success with eight studio albums over ten years. Their 1969 debut, Led Zeppelin, was a top-ten album in several countries and features such tracks as “Good Times Bad Times”, “Dazed and Confused” and “Communication Breakdown”. Led Zeppelin II (1969), their first number-one album, includes “Whole Lotta Love” and “Ramble On”. In 1970, they released Led Zeppelin III which opens with “Immigrant Song”. Their untitled fourth album, commonly known as Led Zeppelin IV (1971), is one of the best-selling albums in history, with 37 million copies sold. It includes “Black Dog”, “Rock and Roll” and “Stairway to Heaven”, with the latter being among the most popular and influential works in rock. Houses of the Holy (1973) includes “The Song Remains the Same” and “The Rain Song”. Physical Graffiti (1975), a double album, features “Trampled Under Foot” and “Kashmir”. Page composed most of Led Zeppelin’s music, while Plant wrote most of the lyrics. Jones occasionally contributed keyboard-focused parts, particularly on the band’s final album. The latter half of their career saw a series of record-breaking tours that earned the group a reputation for excess and debauchery.](https://scontent-sea5-1.cdninstagram.com/v/t51.71878-15/649225864_2459307801166676_2247587835381976500_n.jpg?stp=dst-jpg_e35_s640x640_tt6&_nc_cat=109&ccb=7-5&_nc_sid=18de74&efg=eyJlZmdfdGFnIjoiQ0xJUFMuYmVzdF9pbWFnZV91cmxnZW4uQzMifQ%3D%3D&_nc_ohc=ScG4m3dn_ukQ7kNvwHIvhp-&_nc_oc=AdpkmD9YnRNLXWQs-18LkjZEqo0aDu5jKbQ4Ab21FSNBehIVo26HCCwfBdRioH83GRc&_nc_zt=23&_nc_ht=scontent-sea5-1.cdninstagram.com&_nc_gid=PjTZxFPq-abr304liwTZcw&_nc_ss=7b689&oh=00_AQPeU-piZC2S6xdoYozrWM2XFyKZ6CyyM62txWKbI9uypg&oe=6AC88B4F) [[![Image 18: music.distributor's profile picture](https://scontent-sea5-1.cdninstagram.com/v/t51.82787-19/613726029_17846695140667331_5785330712509894417_n.jpg?stp=dst-jpg_s150x150_tt6&_nc_cat=108&ccb=7-5&_nc_sid=f7ccc5&efg=eyJ2ZW5jb2RlX3RhZyI6InByb2ZpbGVfcGljLnd3dy40NDIuQzMifQ%3D%3D&_nc_ohc=SLa0YzFisfoQ7kNvwHXePsh&_nc_oc=AdolDC0gIavXeKyOIrwpGIIzK3UHLhsrcgbXJhfd7n9FngyTEtW80NYZCtS3mExueUQ&_nc_zt=24&_nc_ht=scontent-sea5-1.cdninstagram.com&_nc_gid=PjTZxFPq-abr304liwTZcw&_nc_ss=7b689&oh=00_AQOroVDOePMj6YNmeCXcwL8TR0X4MWWjp5DbVG8WmdBRyA&oe=6AC872BE)](https://www.instagram.com/music.distributor/)](https://www.instagram.com/music.distributor) [music.distrib...](https://www.instagram.com/music.distributor) 230 Good morning tune goons my girlfriend is actually on a trip in California right now so I thought this song fits my present situation Led Zeppelin were an English rock band formed in London in 1968. [![Image 23: Led Zeppelin at the Gladsaxe Teen Club in Gladsaxe, Denmark March 17, 1969 The famous live television broadcast of Led Zeppelin performing at TV BYEN for Danmarks Radio, recorded on March 17, 1969. At this point in history, the band was still in its infancy, having released their debut album only two months prior. ## What is a Crossword Clue?

According to [The New York Times](link_63), a crossword clue is “a hint that the solver must decipher to find the answer that is then entered into the puzzle grid.” Depending on the puzzle type, clues can range from synonyms to definitions, from puns to wordplay and from general knowledge to fill-in-the-blanks. The possibilities are endless.

If you already have an answer to a clue, use the Crossword Clue tool above to search for clues that have the same answer.

## What is a Crossword Answer?

When you solve for a clue, the resulting word or phrase is the answer, sometimes called a “fill”. Fills can range from one word to multiple words. When you have solved for all clues in a puzzle, all of the answers contribute to a completed puzzle.

If you’re stuck on a crossword clue and can’t decipher and answer, don’t worry! Plug your clue into the [Crossword Solver](link_1) to search through millions of clue/answer pairs for a possible solution.

# Kai Bird

![Image 1: Kai Bird](https://d28hgpri8am2if.cloudfront.net/author_images/28116468/kai-bird-1317405.jpg)

© Photo Mission Studios Ltd.

## About The Author

 Kai Bird is an acclaimed biographer and journalist. With Martin J. Sherwin, he won the Pulitzer Prize for biography for _American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer_, which was the inspiration for Christopher Nolan’s Academy Award–winning Best Picture, _Oppenheimer_. Bird is Executive Director of the Leon Levy Center for Biography at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City. He has won the National Book Critics Circle Award and the Duff Cooper Prize for History and is the recipient of numerous fellowships. His work includes critical writings on the Vietnam War, Hiroshima, nuclear weapons, the Cold War, the Arab-Israeli conflict, and the CIA. He is an elected member of the prestigious Society of American Historians.

 Kerry Douglas Dye is a filmmaker, screenwriter, and amateur baker based in New York City. He’s the author of the middle grade novel _Grady Jones and the Great Detective Game_. # A Must-Listen Podcast for Readers

_The Write Reasons_ is Simon & Schuster's first video podcast. Each month, authors and editors engage in dynamic conversations surrounding our most impactful books and the work they do to bring them to readers’ shelves.

How does an editor decide which book to acquire? What does collaboration look like at a publishing house? Why does a writer write? Explore all these questions and more on _The Write Reasons_, a podcast by Simon & Schuster!
